Discussion (model answer). Dropout randomly removes hidden units during training, so no unit can rely on specific partners being present. That breaks up co-adapted, memorizing feature combinations, and training becomes an implicit average over many thinned networks. Moderate dropout (0.25–0.5) reduces the gap clearly and improves validation accuracy and loss; p = 0.7 removes so much capacity that the network underfits within the 25-epoch budget. Input dropout acts more like pixel noise and helps less.
Forgetting model.eval() leaves dropout active at prediction time. Each prediction then comes from one random thinned network instead of the full network (PyTorch rescales kept units by 1/(1−p) during training so that the full network matches the average), so accuracy drops and results change from run to run. Averaging 20 such passes (MC dropout) recovers the accuracy of the deterministic model and often gives slightly better validation loss and ECE, at 20 times the inference cost. In networks with BatchNorm, MC dropout must switch on only the dropout layers, not BatchNorm’s training mode.

title: Assignment: Improving Generalization in Deep Learning — Solution
text:
Part 10: Noise on weights
At every training step, perturb the weights, compute the gradient at the perturbed point, restore the original weights, then take the optimizer step.
\[
\tilde{w} = w + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, (\sigma\, |w|)^2\right)
\]

Noise is relative to each weight’s magnitude. Sweep σ ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1}; σ = 0 is the baseline.
Noise is applied to weight matrices only, not biases or BatchNorm parameters. Fresh noise is drawn every step, and the clean weights are restored before the update, so noise never accumulates.
Validation always uses the clean weights.


rows = []
for sigma in [0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1]:
    seed = 0
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Flatten(),
        nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Linear(512, 256),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Linear(256, 100),
    ).to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    weight_matrices = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.dim() > 1]      # not biases (or BatchNorm parameters)
    train_loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(Xtr, Ytr), batch_size=128, shuffle=True,
                              generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed))
    history = {"train_loss": [], "train_acc": [], "val_loss": [], "val_acc": []}
    start = time.time()
    for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
        model.train()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        for inputs, targets in train_loader:
            inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
            clean_weights = [w.detach().clone() for w in weight_matrices]
            with torch.no_grad():
                for w in weight_matrices:
                    w.add_(sigma * w.abs() * torch.randn_like(w))
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
            loss.backward()
            with torch.no_grad():                  # gradient was computed at the noisy weights; update the clean ones
                for w, clean in zip(weight_matrices, clean_weights):
                    w.copy_(clean)
            optimizer.step()
            loss_sum += loss.item() * len(targets)
            correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
            count += len(targets)
        history["train_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["train_acc"].append(correct / count)

        model.eval()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for inputs, targets in val_loader:
                inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
                outputs = model(inputs)
                loss_sum += F.cross_entropy(outputs, targets).item() * len(targets)
                correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
                count += len(targets)
        history["val_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["val_acc"].append(correct / count)
    train_time = time.time() - start
    rows.append({"sigma": sigma, "seed": seed, "train_acc": history["train_acc"][-1], "val_acc": history["val_acc"][-1],
                 "val_loss": history["val_loss"][-1], "gap": history["train_acc"][-1] - history["val_acc"][-1],
                 "train_time_s": round(train_time, 1)})
sweep_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(sweep_df.round(4))
best_wn = sweep_df.loc[sweep_df.val_acc.idxmax(), "sigma"]
print("best σ:", best_wn)

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
labels = [str(v) for v in sweep_df["sigma"]]
axs[0].plot(labels, 100 * sweep_df.val_acc, "o-", label="validation")
axs[0].plot(labels, 100 * sweep_df.train_acc, "s--", label="train")
axs[0].set_ylabel("accuracy (%)")
axs[0].legend()
axs[1].plot(labels, sweep_df.val_loss, "o-")
axs[1].set_ylabel("validation loss")
axs[2].plot(labels, 100 * sweep_df.gap, "o-")
axs[2].set_ylabel("train − validation accuracy (pts)")
for ax in axs:
    ax.set_xlabel("sigma")
fig.suptitle("Multiplicative Gaussian noise on weights")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


rows = []
for seed in SEEDS:
    sigma = best_wn
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Flatten(),
        nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Linear(512, 256),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Linear(256, 100),
    ).to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    weight_matrices = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.dim() > 1]      # not biases (or BatchNorm parameters)
    train_loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(Xtr, Ytr), batch_size=128, shuffle=True,
                              generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed))
    history = {"train_loss": [], "train_acc": [], "val_loss": [], "val_acc": []}
    start = time.time()
    for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
        model.train()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        for inputs, targets in train_loader:
            inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
            clean_weights = [w.detach().clone() for w in weight_matrices]
            with torch.no_grad():
                for w in weight_matrices:
                    w.add_(sigma * w.abs() * torch.randn_like(w))
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
            loss.backward()
            with torch.no_grad():                  # gradient was computed at the noisy weights; update the clean ones
                for w, clean in zip(weight_matrices, clean_weights):
                    w.copy_(clean)
            optimizer.step()
            loss_sum += loss.item() * len(targets)
            correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
            count += len(targets)
        history["train_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["train_acc"].append(correct / count)

        model.eval()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for inputs, targets in val_loader:
                inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
                outputs = model(inputs)
                loss_sum += F.cross_entropy(outputs, targets).item() * len(targets)
                correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
                count += len(targets)
        history["val_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["val_acc"].append(correct / count)
    train_time = time.time() - start
    rows.append({"seed": seed, "train_acc": history["train_acc"][-1], "val_acc": history["val_acc"][-1],
                 "val_loss": history["val_loss"][-1], "gap": history["train_acc"][-1] - history["val_acc"][-1],
                 "train_time_s": round(train_time, 1)})
label = f"weight noise, σ={best_wn}"

seed_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(seed_df.round(4))
print(f"{label}: validation accuracy {100 * seed_df.val_acc.mean():.2f} ± {100 * seed_df.val_acc.std():.2f} %, "
      f"validation loss {seed_df.val_loss.mean():.3f} ± {seed_df.val_loss.std():.3f}, "
      f"gap {100 * seed_df.gap.mean():.1f} pts")

Discussion (model answer).
Flat minima. Averaged over the noise, the training objective becomes \(\mathbb{E}_\epsilon[L(w+\epsilon)] \approx L(w) + \tfrac12\sum_i \sigma^2 w_i^2\, \partial^2 L/\partial w_i^2\). The extra term penalizes curvature of the loss along each weight, scaled by the weight’s size, so the optimizer is rewarded for solutions where the loss stays low in a neighbourhood of w. Such flat minima tend to generalize better (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997); sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) is the worst-case version of the same idea.
Results. σ = 0.001 is too small to matter. Moderate σ gives a small reduction in the gap; the effect is usually smaller than dropout’s, whose noise is much larger (it zeroes whole units). Large σ makes the gradients noisy enough to slow learning and lowers accuracy.
Why not BatchNorm. BatchNorm’s scale γ and shift β multiply or offset an entire channel, so noise on them perturbs every unit in the channel at once, a much larger effect than independent noise on individual connections, and it destabilizes training. BatchNorm’s running statistics are not trained parameters and must stay clean. This MLP has no BatchNorm, but the code follows the same rule (only parameters with two or more dimensions are perturbed).

title: Assignment: Improving Generalization in Deep Learning — Solution
section: Part 11: Best combined model, ablation, and final test evaluation
text:
Part 11: Best combined model, ablation, and final test evaluation

Combine at least four techniques at their best validation settings. Fill in COMBINED from your Parts 1–10 results; the values below are placeholders. Transfer learning and ensembling are left out so the combined model stays an MLP (needed for the fair comparison in Part 12); ensembling can be applied on top of any model. Multi-task learning is left out to keep the training loop simple; add it if it helped in Part 6.
Leave-one-out ablation: switch off each technique in turn and retrain with all seeds.
Identify redundant or interfering techniques.
Freeze every choice, then evaluate on the test set once: accuracy, loss, ECE, a reliability diagram, and robustness to Gaussian input noise at two severities chosen in advance.


from torchvision import transforms


class AugmentedDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y, transform):
        self.X, self.y, self.transform = X, y, transform

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.y)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.transform(self.X[i]), self.y[i]


crop_and_flip = transforms.Compose([transforms.RandomCrop(32, padding=4), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip()])


def train_config(config, seed, epochs=EPOCHS, train_positions=None):
    """Trains the MLP with whichever techniques are switched on in `config`.
    Returns the trained model, its history, and the train/validation numbers of the returned weights."""
    X, Y = Xtr, Ytr
    if train_positions is not None:
        X, Y = Xtr[train_positions], Ytr[train_positions]
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    p = config["dropout"]
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Flatten(),
        nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Dropout(p),
        nn.Linear(512, 256),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Dropout(p),
        nn.Linear(256, 100),
    ).to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=config["weight_decay"])
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=config["label_smoothing"])
    dataset = AugmentedDataset(X, Y, crop_and_flip) if config["augment"] else TensorDataset(X, Y)
    train_loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed))
    weight_matrices = [w for w in model.parameters() if w.dim() > 1]
    history = {"train_loss": [], "train_acc": [], "val_loss": [], "val_acc": []}
    best_loss, best_epoch, wait = float("inf"), 0, 0
    best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
    start = time.time()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        for inputs, targets in train_loader:
            inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
            if config["input_noise"] > 0:
                inputs = inputs + config["input_noise"] * torch.randn_like(inputs)
            if config["weight_noise"] > 0:
                clean_weights = [w.detach().clone() for w in weight_matrices]
                with torch.no_grad():
                    for w in weight_matrices:
                        w.add_(config["weight_noise"] * w.abs() * torch.randn_like(w))
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
            loss.backward()
            if config["weight_noise"] > 0:
                with torch.no_grad():
                    for w, clean in zip(weight_matrices, clean_weights):
                        w.copy_(clean)
            optimizer.step()
            loss_sum += loss.item() * len(targets)
            correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
            count += len(targets)
        history["train_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["train_acc"].append(correct / count)

        model.eval()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for inputs, targets in val_loader:
                inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
                outputs = model(inputs)
                loss_sum += F.cross_entropy(outputs, targets).item() * len(targets)
                correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
                count += len(targets)
        history["val_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["val_acc"].append(correct / count)

        if history["val_loss"][-1] < best_loss:
            best_loss, best_epoch, wait = history["val_loss"][-1], epoch + 1, 0
            best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        else:
            wait += 1
            if config["patience"] is not None and wait >= config["patience"]:
                break
    train_time = time.time() - start
    final = len(history["val_acc"]) - 1
    if config["patience"] is not None:
        model.load_state_dict(best_state)
        final = best_epoch - 1
    model.eval()
    result = {"seed": seed, "train_acc": history["train_acc"][final], "val_acc": history["val_acc"][final],
              "val_loss": history["val_loss"][final], "gap": history["train_acc"][final] - history["val_acc"][final],
              "train_time_s": round(train_time, 1)}
    return model, history, result

BASELINE = {"augment": False, "dropout": 0.0, "label_smoothing": 0.0, "weight_decay": 0.0,
            "input_noise": 0.0, "weight_noise": 0.0, "patience": None}
# The techniques that beat the baseline on validation in Parts 1–10, at their best settings.
# These defaults are placeholders: replace them with your own results (at least four techniques switched on).
COMBINED = {"augment": True, "dropout": 0.25, "label_smoothing": 0.1, "weight_decay": 0.05,
            "input_noise": 0.0, "weight_noise": 0.0, "patience": None}


def describe(config):
    on = [k for k, v in config.items() if v not in (False, 0, 0.0, None)]
    return ", ".join(f"{k}={config[k]}" for k in on) or "baseline"


baseline_models, combined_models, rows = [], [], []
for name, config, keep in [("baseline", BASELINE, baseline_models), ("full combined model", COMBINED, combined_models)]:
    results = []
    for seed in SEEDS:
        model, history, result = train_config(config, seed)
        keep.append(model)
        results.append(result)
    res = pd.DataFrame(results)
    rows.append({"configuration": name, "settings": describe(config),
                 "val_acc": res.val_acc.mean(), "val_acc_sd": res.val_acc.std(), "val_loss": res.val_loss.mean(),
                 "gap": res.gap.mean()})

# Leave-one-out ablation: switch off one technique at a time
switched_on = [k for k, v in COMBINED.items() if v not in (False, 0, 0.0, None)]
for technique in switched_on:
    config = dict(COMBINED)
    config[technique] = BASELINE[technique]
    results = pd.DataFrame([train_config(config, seed)[2] for seed in SEEDS])
    rows.append({"configuration": f"− {technique}", "settings": describe(config),
                 "val_acc": results.val_acc.mean(), "val_acc_sd": results.val_acc.std(),
                 "val_loss": results.val_loss.mean(), "gap": results.gap.mean()})

ablation = pd.DataFrame(rows)
full_acc = ablation.loc[ablation.configuration == "full combined model", "val_acc"].item()
ablation["Δ vs full (pts)"] = (100 * (ablation.val_acc - full_acc)).round(2)
display(ablation.round(4))

Reading the ablation. A negative Δ means removing the technique hurt, so it contributes. A Δ within about one standard deviation of zero means it is redundant given the others. A positive Δ means it interferes: the model is better without it.
Discussion (model answer): interactions. Techniques tuned one at a time rarely add up, because several regularize through the same channel:

Augmentation and input noise both perturb the inputs; once crops and flips are present, extra pixel noise adds little.
Label smoothing and Mixup both soften the targets; together they make the network underconfident.
Heavy augmentation and large dropout both slow fitting. Within a fixed epoch budget, stacking them can push the model into underfitting, visible as training accuracy barely above validation accuracy.
Early stopping and augmentation: with augmentation, validation loss reaches its minimum much later, so the patience chosen without augmentation can stop training too soon.
Weight decay and dropout both reduce effective capacity; strengths tuned individually are usually too strong in combination.

The fix is to retune a few of the combined strengths together (for example, halve dropout and weight decay) on the validation set, which is still allowed because the test set has not been used.

# ===================== FINAL TEST EVALUATION: run once, after every choice above is frozen =====================
# Uses `baseline_models` and `combined_models` from the cell above.
NOISE_SEVERITIES = [0.04, 0.08]      # std of Gaussian noise in [0, 1] pixel units, chosen before testing

test_sets = {}
for severity in [0.0] + NOISE_SEVERITIES:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
    images = X_test.astype(np.float32) / 255
    if severity > 0:
        images = np.clip(images + rng.normal(0, severity, images.shape).astype(np.float32), 0, 1)
    x = ((torch.tensor(images) - MEAN) / STD).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).contiguous()
    test_sets["clean" if severity == 0 else f"noise σ={severity}"] = x
Yte = torch.tensor(yf_test)

rows, test_probs = [], {}
for name, models_list in [("baseline", baseline_models), ("combined", combined_models)]:
    for set_name, X in test_sets.items():
        per_seed = []
        for model in models_list:
            model.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                probs = torch.cat([F.softmax(model(X[i:i + 1000].to(device)), 1).cpu() for i in range(0, len(X), 1000)])
            if set_name == "clean":
                test_probs.setdefault(name, probs)
            correct = (probs.argmax(1) == Yte).float()
            confidence = probs.max(1).values
            ece = 0.0
            bin_edges = torch.linspace(0, 1, 16)
            for lo, hi in zip(bin_edges[:-1], bin_edges[1:]):
                in_bin = (confidence > lo) & (confidence <= hi)
                if in_bin.any():
                    ece += in_bin.float().mean().item() * abs(confidence[in_bin].mean().item() - correct[in_bin].mean().item())
            per_seed.append({"acc": correct.mean().item(),
                             "loss": -torch.log(probs[torch.arange(len(Yte)), Yte].clamp_min(1e-12)).mean().item(),
                             "ECE": ece})
        df = pd.DataFrame(per_seed)
        rows.append({"model": name, "test set": set_name,
                     "test acc (%)": f"{100 * df.acc.mean():.2f} ± {100 * df.acc.std():.2f}",
                     "test loss": f"{df.loss.mean():.3f} ± {df.loss.std():.3f}",
                     "test ECE": f"{df.ECE.mean():.3f} ± {df.ECE.std():.3f}"})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.5))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ":", color="gray")
for name, probs in test_probs.items():
    confidence, prediction = probs.max(dim=1)
    correct = (prediction == Yte).float()
    xs, ys = [], []
    for lo, hi in zip(bin_edges[:-1], bin_edges[1:]):
        in_bin = (confidence > lo) & (confidence <= hi)
        if in_bin.any():
            xs.append(confidence[in_bin].mean().item())
            ys.append(correct[in_bin].mean().item())
    ax.plot(xs, ys, "o-", label=name)
ax.set_xlabel("confidence"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_title("Reliability on the test set (first seed)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Discussion (model answer). The combined model should beat the baseline on clean test accuracy by a margin several times larger than the seed-to-seed standard deviation, with much lower loss and ECE; test numbers track validation numbers closely because nothing was tuned on the test set. Its reliability curve sits much closer to the diagonal. Under Gaussian noise both models lose accuracy as severity increases, but the combined model typically degrades less, especially if it includes input noise or augmentation, because those train it on perturbed images. If a group’s combined model does not beat the baseline, the ablation table is the evidence for why (usually interference), and that is an acceptable, gradable result.

title: Assignment: Improving Generalization in Deep Learning — Solution
section: Part 12: Does regularization matter at scale? Scaling and compute
text:
Part 12: Does regularization matter at scale? Scaling and compute
Regularization is most valuable when data is scarce; this part measures how that changes as the training set grows.

Train the baseline and the combined model (an MLP, no transfer learning) on nested, stratified 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% subsets of the training split. The validation set stays fixed. Early stopping is turned off here so that training budgets are exactly controlled. Set COMBINED to the same settings as in Part 11.
Two budgets: fixed epochs (smaller subsets also get fewer optimizer steps) and fixed steps (every subset gets as many optimizer steps as the full data). Comparing them separates the effect of more data from the effect of more optimization.
One seed per point. Report throughput and total training time.


from torchvision import transforms


class AugmentedDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y, transform):
        self.X, self.y, self.transform = X, y, transform

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.y)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.transform(self.X[i]), self.y[i]


crop_and_flip = transforms.Compose([transforms.RandomCrop(32, padding=4), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip()])


def train_config(config, seed, epochs=EPOCHS, train_positions=None):
    """Trains the MLP with whichever techniques are switched on in `config`.
    Returns the trained model, its history, and the train/validation numbers of the returned weights."""
    X, Y = Xtr, Ytr
    if train_positions is not None:
        X, Y = Xtr[train_positions], Ytr[train_positions]
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    p = config["dropout"]
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Flatten(),
        nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Dropout(p),
        nn.Linear(512, 256),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Dropout(p),
        nn.Linear(256, 100),
    ).to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=config["weight_decay"])
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=config["label_smoothing"])
    dataset = AugmentedDataset(X, Y, crop_and_flip) if config["augment"] else TensorDataset(X, Y)
    train_loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed))
    weight_matrices = [w for w in model.parameters() if w.dim() > 1]
    history = {"train_loss": [], "train_acc": [], "val_loss": [], "val_acc": []}
    best_loss, best_epoch, wait = float("inf"), 0, 0
    best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
    start = time.time()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        for inputs, targets in train_loader:
            inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
            if config["input_noise"] > 0:
                inputs = inputs + config["input_noise"] * torch.randn_like(inputs)
            if config["weight_noise"] > 0:
                clean_weights = [w.detach().clone() for w in weight_matrices]
                with torch.no_grad():
                    for w in weight_matrices:
                        w.add_(config["weight_noise"] * w.abs() * torch.randn_like(w))
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
            loss.backward()
            if config["weight_noise"] > 0:
                with torch.no_grad():
                    for w, clean in zip(weight_matrices, clean_weights):
                        w.copy_(clean)
            optimizer.step()
            loss_sum += loss.item() * len(targets)
            correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
            count += len(targets)
        history["train_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["train_acc"].append(correct / count)

        model.eval()
        loss_sum, correct, count = 0.0, 0, 0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for inputs, targets in val_loader:
                inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
                outputs = model(inputs)
                loss_sum += F.cross_entropy(outputs, targets).item() * len(targets)
                correct += (outputs.argmax(1) == targets).sum().item()
                count += len(targets)
        history["val_loss"].append(loss_sum / count)
        history["val_acc"].append(correct / count)

        if history["val_loss"][-1] < best_loss:
            best_loss, best_epoch, wait = history["val_loss"][-1], epoch + 1, 0
            best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        else:
            wait += 1
            if config["patience"] is not None and wait >= config["patience"]:
                break
    train_time = time.time() - start
    final = len(history["val_acc"]) - 1
    if config["patience"] is not None:
        model.load_state_dict(best_state)
        final = best_epoch - 1
    model.eval()
    result = {"seed": seed, "train_acc": history["train_acc"][final], "val_acc": history["val_acc"][final],
              "val_loss": history["val_loss"][final], "gap": history["train_acc"][final] - history["val_acc"][final],
              "train_time_s": round(train_time, 1)}
    return model, history, result

BASELINE = {"augment": False, "dropout": 0.0, "label_smoothing": 0.0, "weight_decay": 0.0,
            "input_noise": 0.0, "weight_noise": 0.0, "patience": None}
# The techniques that beat the baseline on validation in Parts 1–10, at their best settings.
# These defaults are placeholders: replace them with your own results (at least four techniques switched on).
COMBINED = {"augment": True, "dropout": 0.25, "label_smoothing": 0.1, "weight_decay": 0.05,
            "input_noise": 0.0, "weight_noise": 0.0, "patience": None}
COMBINED["patience"] = None          # no early stopping here, so budgets are exactly controlled

# Nested stratified subsets: the same per-class shuffle, so 10% ⊂ 25% ⊂ 50% ⊂ 100%
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
labels = Ytr.numpy()
class_orders = [rng.permutation(np.flatnonzero(labels == c)) for c in range(100)]

rows = []
for frac in [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]:
    positions = np.sort(np.concatenate([order[: max(1, round(frac * len(order)))] for order in class_orders]))
    for name, config in [("baseline", BASELINE), ("combined", COMBINED)]:
        for budget, epochs in [("fixed epochs", EPOCHS), ("fixed steps", round(EPOCHS / frac))]:
            if frac == 1.0 and budget == "fixed steps":
                continue                              # identical to fixed epochs at 100%
            model, history, result = train_config(config, seed=0, epochs=epochs, train_positions=positions)
            row = {"model": name, "budget": budget, "n_train": len(positions), "epochs": epochs,
                   "steps": epochs * math.ceil(len(positions) / 128), **result,
                   "images/s": round(epochs * len(positions) / result["train_time_s"])}
            rows.append(row)
            if frac == 1.0:
                rows.append({**row, "budget": "fixed steps"})
scale_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(scale_df.drop(columns="seed").round(4))

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.2))
for (name, budget), g in scale_df.groupby(["model", "budget"]):
    style = "o-" if budget == "fixed steps" else "o--"
    axs[0].plot(g.n_train, 100 * g.val_acc, style, label=f"{name}, {budget}")
    axs[1].plot(g.n_train, 100 * g.gap, style, label=f"{name}, {budget}")
    axs[2].plot(g.train_time_s, 100 * g.val_acc, style, label=f"{name}, {budget}")
axs[0].set_ylabel("validation accuracy (%)"); axs[1].set_ylabel("train − validation accuracy (pts)")
axs[2].set_ylabel("validation accuracy (%)"); axs[2].set_xlabel("training time (s)")
for ax in axs[:2]:
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("training images (log scale)")
for ax in axs:
    ax.legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Extrapolation: fit baseline accuracy ≈ a + b·ln(n) under fixed steps, and solve for the n at which the baseline
# would match the combined model's accuracy at the smallest subset.
g = scale_df[(scale_df.model == "baseline") & (scale_df.budget == "fixed steps")].sort_values("n_train")
b, a = np.polyfit(np.log(g.n_train), g.val_acc, 1)
smallest = scale_df[(scale_df.model == "combined") & (scale_df.budget == "fixed steps")].sort_values("n_train").iloc[0]
n_needed = math.exp((smallest.val_acc - a) / b) if b > 0 else float("nan")
if b > 0 and n_needed > smallest.n_train:
    print(f"combined model with {smallest.n_train} images: {smallest.val_acc:.2%}. The fit says the baseline would need "
          f"about {n_needed:,.0f} images to match it ({n_needed / smallest.n_train:.1f}× more data).")
else:
    print("At the smallest subset the combined model does not beat the baseline, so there is nothing to extrapolate.")

device_name = torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if device.type == "cuda" else str(device)
print(f"\nhardware: {device_name} | batch size 128 | total training time in this part: "
      f"{scale_df.drop_duplicates(['model', 'n_train', 'epochs']).train_time_s.sum() / 3600:.2f} hours")


# Data loading throughput: does loading with parallel workers help? (loading and moving to the device only, no model)
from torchvision import transforms


class AugmentedDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y, transform):
        self.X, self.y, self.transform = X, y, transform

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.y)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.transform(self.X[i]), self.y[i]


crop_and_flip = transforms.Compose([transforms.RandomCrop(32, padding=4), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip()])
for name, dataset in [("no augmentation", TensorDataset(Xtr, Ytr)), ("crop + flip", AugmentedDataset(Xtr, Ytr, crop_and_flip))]:
    for workers in [0, 2]:
        try:
            loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, num_workers=workers,
                                pin_memory=device.type == "cuda")
            start = time.time()
            for inputs, targets in loader:
                inputs = inputs.to(device)
            print(f"{name}, num_workers={workers}: {len(dataset) / (time.time() - start):,.0f} images/s")
        except Exception as e:      # some notebook environments (for example macOS) cannot start worker processes
            print(f"{name}, num_workers={workers}: not available here ({type(e).__name__})")

Discussion (model answer).
Does the regularization gap shrink with data? Yes. Under fixed steps, both models improve roughly linearly in log(training images), and the baseline improves faster, so the distance between the curves narrows as data grows. The baseline’s train − validation gap also shrinks, because 40,000 images are harder to memorize than 4,000. Regularization is a substitute for data: the combined model at a small subset matches what the extrapolated baseline only reaches with several times more images (the cell prints the estimate, which is a rough guide fitted to four points).
Data vs. steps. Under fixed epochs, the small subsets also receive far fewer optimizer steps, so their low accuracy mixes “less data” with “less training”. The fixed-steps curves remove that confound. For the baseline, extra steps on a small subset mostly increase overfitting (high training accuracy, unchanged validation accuracy), which shows that the limit at small n is data, not optimization.
What to prioritize at 100× the data. 1. Transfer learning / pretraining stays the most valuable, because it brings in information from outside the dataset. 2. Data augmentation stays useful. It encodes invariances (shift, mirror) that more data covers only gradually, and large vision models are still trained with heavy augmentation. 3. Weight decay is free and remains standard. 4. Early stopping becomes a compute-saving tool more than a regularizer. 5. Dropout and label smoothing matter less as overfitting fades, and ensembling becomes the most expensive option, since every member must be trained on the full data.
Throughput. Per-image augmentation in a Dataset costs CPU time, and loader worker processes help when that becomes the bottleneck; for data that does not fit in memory, parallel loading is essential.
Limitations. CIFAR-100 fits in memory and trains in minutes, so it cannot show the problems that dominate at real scale: I/O and storage throughput, distributed training, data deduplication, label noise and long-tailed classes. The trends here (regularization matters less with more data; augmentation and pretraining keep mattering) are consistent with large-scale results, but the magnitudes do not transfer.

title: Fall 2026 CSC-372 Project Part 7
text:
0. Establish a baseline
Build a sequential feed-forward neural network model and train it from random initialization using cross-entropy loss.
For the baseline:

Normalize the input images.
Use no data augmentation, dropout, label smoothing, injected noise, or weight decay.
Train for a fixed number of epochs.
Save training and validation loss and accuracy after every epoch.
Keep model size and training budget practical for repeated experiments.

Choose the optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, and epoch budget before the main experiments. Keep them fixed unless a method requires a documented change.
Report parameter count, training time, training accuracy, validation accuracy, and the generalization gap:

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from PIL import Image
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from torchvision import transforms

images = ds["train"]["img"]
labels = ds["train"]["fine_label"]

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
indices = rng.permutation(len(images))
val_indices = indices[:10_000]
train_indices = indices[10_000:]

X_valid = [images[int(i)] for i in val_indices]
y_valid = [labels[int(i)] for i in val_indices]
X_train = [images[int(i)] for i in train_indices]
y_train = [labels[int(i)] for i in train_indices]


class MyDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.features = X
        self.labels = y
        self.transform = transforms.Compose([
            transforms.ToTensor(),
            transforms.Normalize(
                (0.5071, 0.4867, 0.4408),
                (0.2675, 0.2565, 0.2761)
            ),
        ])

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        image = self.features[index]

        # Handles PIL images or original uint8 image arrays.
        if not isinstance(image, Image.Image):
            image = Image.fromarray(np.asarray(image))

        image = self.transform(image.convert("RGB"))
        label = torch.tensor(int(self.labels[index]), dtype=torch.long)
        return image, label

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.features)


train_dataset = MyDataset(X_train, y_train)
val_dataset = MyDataset(X_valid, y_valid)

train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True
)
val_loader = DataLoader(
    val_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=False
)

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    device = torch.device("cuda")
elif torch.backends.mps.is_available():
    device = torch.device("mps")
else:
    device = torch.device("cpu")



model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(512, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 100),
).to(device)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

num_epochs = 25

train_loss_history = []
val_loss_history = []

train_accuracy_history = []
val_accuracy_history = []

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    train_loss_sum = 0.0
    train_correct = 0
    train_count = 0

    for inputs, targets in train_loader:
        inputs = inputs.to(device)
        targets = targets.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        batch_size = targets.size(0)
        train_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
        train_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
        train_count += batch_size

    model.eval()
    val_loss_sum = 0.0
    val_correct = 0
    val_count = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, targets in val_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            targets = targets.to(device)

            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

            batch_size = targets.size(0)
            val_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
            val_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
            val_count += batch_size

    train_loss_history.append(train_loss_sum / train_count)
    val_loss_history.append(val_loss_sum / val_count)

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch + 1}/{num_epochs} | "
        f"Train loss: {train_loss_sum / train_count:.4f} | "
        f"Train accuracy: {train_correct / train_count:.2%} | "
        f"Val loss: {val_loss_sum / val_count:.4f} | "
        f"Val accuracy: {val_correct / val_count:.2%}"
    )

    train_accuracy_history.append(train_correct / train_count)
    val_accuracy_history.append(val_correct / val_count)

Epoch 1/25 | Train loss: 3.8296 | Train accuracy: 12.50% | Val loss: 3.6093 | Val accuracy: 16.26%
Epoch 2/25 | Train loss: 3.4446 | Train accuracy: 18.59% | Val loss: 3.4817 | Val accuracy: 18.95%

Choose the optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, and epoch budget before the main experiments. Keep them fixed unless a method requires a documented change.
Note that transforms.Compose combines image transformations into a sequence and applies them in the order listed whenever an image is loaded. In this notebook, it converts images into PyTorch tensors using ToTensor() and normalizes each color channel using Normalize(). For data augmentation, we add transformations such as random crops and horizontal flips before ToTensor(). These random transformations can produce a different version of an image each time it is loaded during training. For validation and testing, we use only conversion and normalization so that evaluation images are not randomly altered.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from PIL import Image
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from torchvision import transforms

images = ds["train"]["img"]
labels = ds["train"]["fine_label"]

# Reuse the existing stratified split.
X_train = train_ds["img"]
y_train = train_ds["fine_label"]

X_valid = valid_ds["img"]
y_valid = valid_ds["fine_label"]

X_test = test_ds["img"]
y_test = test_ds["fine_label"]


class MyDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.features = X
        self.labels = y
        self.transform = transforms.Compose([
            transforms.ToTensor(),
            transforms.Normalize(
                (0.5071, 0.4867, 0.4408),
                (0.2675, 0.2565, 0.2761)
            ),
        ])

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        image = self.features[index]

        # Handles PIL images or original uint8 image arrays.
        if not isinstance(image, Image.Image):
            image = Image.fromarray(np.asarray(image))

        image = self.transform(image.convert("RGB"))
        label = torch.tensor(int(self.labels[index]), dtype=torch.long)
        return image, label

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.features)


train_dataset = MyDataset(X_train, y_train)
val_dataset = MyDataset(X_valid, y_valid)

train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True
)
val_loader = DataLoader(
    val_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=False
)

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    device = torch.device("cuda")
elif torch.backends.mps.is_available():
    device = torch.device("mps")
else:
    device = torch.device("cpu")



model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(512, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 100),
).to(device)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

num_epochs = 25

train_loss_history = []
val_loss_history = []

train_accuracy_history = []
val_accuracy_history = []

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    train_loss_sum = 0.0
    train_correct = 0
    train_count = 0

    for inputs, targets in train_loader:
        inputs = inputs.to(device)
        targets = targets.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        batch_size = targets.size(0)
        train_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
        train_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
        train_count += batch_size

    model.eval()
    val_loss_sum = 0.0
    val_correct = 0
    val_count = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, targets in val_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            targets = targets.to(device)

            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

            batch_size = targets.size(0)
            val_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
            val_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
            val_count += batch_size

    train_loss_history.append(train_loss_sum / train_count)
    val_loss_history.append(val_loss_sum / val_count)

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch + 1}/{num_epochs} | "
        f"Train loss: {train_loss_sum / train_count:.4f} | "
        f"Train accuracy: {train_correct / train_count:.2%} | "
        f"Val loss: {val_loss_sum / val_count:.4f} | "
        f"Val accuracy: {val_correct / val_count:.2%}"
    )

    train_accuracy_history.append(train_correct / train_count)
    val_accuracy_history.append(val_correct / val_count)

Decoder model example: GPT3
This section presents a high-level description of GPT3, an example of a decoder model. The basic architecture is extremely similar to the encoder model and comprises a series of transformer layers that operate on learned word embeddings. However, the goal is different. The encoder aimed to build a representation of the text that could be fine- tuned to solve a variety of more specific NLP tasks. Conversely, the decoder has one purpose: to generate the next token in a sequence. It can generate a coherent text passage by feeding the extended sequence back into the model.

Language modeling
GPT3 is an autoregressive language model. This is easiest to understand with a concrete example. Consider the sentence

It takes great courage to let yourself appear weak.

For simplicity, let’s assume that the tokens are the full words. The probability of the full sentence can be factored as:
\[\begin{eqnarray}
  Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let yourself appear weak}}) &=&\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{takes}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{great}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{courage}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great}})\times\nonumber \\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{to}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{let}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to}})\times\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{yourself}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let}})\times\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{appear}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let yourself}})\times\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{weak}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let yourself appear}}).
\end{eqnarray}\]
An autoregressive model predicts the conditional distributions \(Pr(t_n|t_1,...,t_{n-1})\) of each token given all the prior tokens, and hence indirectly computes the joint proba- bility \(Pr(t_1,t_2,...,t_N )\) of all \(N\) tokens:
\[\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq:transformer_autoregressive}
  Pr(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots, t_{N}) = Pr(t_{1})\prod_{n=2}^{N}Pr(t_{n}|t_{1},\ldots, t_{n-1}).
\end{eqnarray}\]
The autoregressive formulation demonstrates the connection between maximizing the joint probability of the tokens and the next token prediction task.


Masked self-attention
To train a decoder, we seek parameters that maximize the log probability of the input text under the autoregressive model (i.e., that maximize the sum of the log conditional probability terms). Ideally, we would pass in the whole sentence and compute all the log probabilities and gradients in the same forward pass rather than doing a forward pass for each token in the sentence. However, if we pass in the full sentence, the term computing log [Pr(great|It takes)] would have access to both the answer great and the right context courage to let yourself appear weak. Hence, the system can cheat rather than learn to predict the following words and won’t train properly.
Fortunately, the tokens only interact in the self-attention layers in a transformer network. Hence, the problem can be resolved by ensuring that the attention to the answer and the right context is zero. This can be achieved by setting the corresponding dot products in the self-attention computation (equation 12.5) to negative infinity before they are passed through the \(\textbf{softmax[•]}\) function. This is known as masked self-attention. The effect is to make the weight of all the upward-angled arrows in figure 12.1 zero.
The entire decoder network operates as follows. The input text is tokenized, and the tokens are converted to embeddings. The embeddings are passed into the transformer network, but now the transformer layers use masked self-attention so that they can only attend to the current and previous tokens. Each of the output embeddings can be thought of as representing a partial sentence, and for each, the goal is to predict the next token in the sequence. Consequently, after the transformer layers, a single linear layer maps each output embedding to the size of the vocabulary, followed by a \(\textbf{softmax[•]}\) function that converts these values to probabilities. During training, we aim to maximize the sum of the log probabilities of the next token in the ground truth sequence at every position using a standard multiclass cross-entropy loss (figure 12.12).


Generating text from a decoder
The autoregressive language model is the first example of a generative model discussed in this book. Since it defines a probability model over text sequences, it can be used to sample new examples of plausible text. To generate from the model, we start with an input sequence of text (which might be just the special  token indicating the beginning of the sequence) and feed this into the network, which then outputs the probabilities over possible subsequent tokens. We can then either pick the most likely token or sample from this probability distribution. The new extended sequence can be fed back into the decoder network to yield the probability distribution over the next token. By repeating this process, we can generate large bodies of text. The computation can be made quite eﬀicient as prior embeddings do not depend on subsequent ones due to the masked self-attention. Hence, much of the earlier computation can be recycled as we generate subsequent tokens.
In practice, many strategies can make the output text more coherent. For example, beam search keeps track of multiple possible sentence completions to find the overall most likely sequence of words (which is not necessarily found by greedily choosing the most likely word at each step). Top-k sampling randomly draws the next word from only the top-K most likely possibilities to prevent the system from accidentally choosing from the long tail of low-probability tokens and leading to an unnecessary linguistic dead end.

Training GPT3-type decoder network. The tokens are mapped to word embeddings with a special  token at the beginning of the sequence. The embeddings are passed through a series of transformer layers that use masked self-attention. Here, each position in the sentence can only attend to its own embedding and those of tokens earlier in the sequence (orange connections). The goal at each position is to maximize the probability of the following ground truth token in the sequence. In other words, at position one, we want to maximize the probability of the token It; at position two, we want to maximize the probability of the token takes; and so on. Masked self-attention ensures the system cannot cheat by looking at subsequent inputs. The autoregressive task has the advantage of making efficient use of the data since every word contributes a term to the loss function. However, it only exploits the left context of each word.


GPT3 and few-shot learning
Large language models like GPT3 apply these ideas on a massive scale. In GPT3, the sequence lengths are 2048 tokens long, and the total batch size is 3.2 million tokens. There are 96 transformer layers (some of which implement a sparse version of attention), each processing a word embedding of size 12288. There are 96 heads in the self-attention layers, and the value, query, and key dimension is 128. It is trained with 300 billion tokens and contains 175 billion parameters.
Here’s an example of completing text from the GPT3 model where the text provided to the model is in orange, and the generated text is in cyan:

Understanding Deep Learning is a new textbook from MIT Press by Simon Prince that’s de- signed to offer an accessible, broad introduction to the field. Deep learning is a branch of machine learning that is concerned with algorithms that learn from data that is unstructured or unlabeled. The book is divided into four sections:

Introduction to deep learning
Deep learning architecture
Deep learning algorithms
Applications of deep learning

The first section offers an introduction to deep learning, including its history and origins. The second section covers deep learning architecture, discussing various types of neural net- works and their applications. The third section dives into deep learning algorithms, including supervised and unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and more. The fourth section applies deep learning to various domains, such as computer vision, natural language processing, and robotics.

This continuation is plausible, albeit only partially accurate. One surprising property of learning models on this scale is that they can perform many tasks without fine-tuning. If we provide several examples of correct question/answer pairs and then another question, they often answer the final question correctly by completing the sequence. One example is correcting English grammar:

Poor English input: I eated the purple berries.
Good English output: I ate the purple berries.
Poor English input: Thank you for picking me as your designer. I’d appreciate it.
Good English output: Thank you for choosing me as your designer. I appreciate it.
Poor English input: The mentioned changes have done. or I did the alteration that you requested. or I changed things you wanted and did the modifications.
Good English output: The requested changes have been made. or I made the alteration that you requested. or I changed things you wanted and made the modifications.
Poor English input: I’d be more than happy to work with you in another project.
Good English output: I’d be more than happy to work with you on another project.
(result from Brown et al., 2020)

Here, the text containing the paired examples in orange was provided as context for GPT3, and the system then generated the correct answer in cyan. This phenomenon extends to many situations, including generating code snippets based on natural language descriptions, arithmetic, translating between languages, and answering questions about text passages. Consequently, it is argued that enormous language models are few-shot learners; they can learn to do novel tasks based on just a few examples. However, performance is erratic in practice, and the extent to which it is extrapolating from learned examples rather than merely interpolating or copying verbatim is unclear.

Encoder-decoder architecture. Two sentences are passed to the system with the goal of translating the first into the second. a) The first sentence is passed through a standard encoder. b) The second sentence is passed through a decoder that uses masked self-attention but also attends to the output embeddings of the encoder using cross-attention (orange rectangle). The loss function is the same as for the decoder model; we want to maximize the probability of the next word in the output sequence.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Dot Product Primer





Click to expand

In machine learning, data points are often represented as vectors in a high-dimensional space. For example, word embeddings represent words as vectors, with semantically related words often occupying nearby regions of the embedding space. To compare two vectors, we need a way to measure how similar they are.
Three commonly used measures are Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, and dot product. Although closely related mathematically, they capture different aspects of the relationship between vectors.


Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between two points in space.
For two vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\):
\[
d(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d}(a_i-b_i)^2}
\]
A smaller distance indicates that the vectors are closer together. Euclidean distance considers both the direction and magnitude of the vectors.



Cosine similarity measures the angle between two nonzero vectors, regardless of their magnitudes.
\[
\cos(\theta)=\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|}
\]

1: Vectors point in the same direction.
0: Vectors are perpendicular.
−1: Vectors point in opposite directions.

For example, the vectors \([1,2]\) and \([10,20]\) have a cosine similarity of 1, even though they are far apart in Euclidean distance.
Cosine similarity is particularly useful when the direction of a vector is more important than its magnitude.



The dot product of two vectors is calculated by multiplying corresponding components and summing the results:
\[
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_i b_i
\]
Geometrically, the dot product can also be expressed as:
\[
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos(\theta)
\]
This reveals an important relationship: the dot product combines angular alignment (cosine similarity) with vector magnitudes.
Two vectors have a large positive dot product when they point in similar directions and have large magnitudes. Their dot product is zero when they are perpendicular and negative when they point in opposing directions.
Unlike cosine similarity, the dot product is not normalized. Consequently, two vectors can have a high dot product because of their magnitudes, even if they are not especially well aligned.



Consider three vectors:
\[
\mathbf{a}=[1,2],\quad \mathbf{b}=[2,4],\quad \mathbf{c}=[-2,1]
\]

Vectors a and b point in exactly the same direction, giving them a cosine similarity of 1, but they have different magnitudes and therefore a nonzero Euclidean distance. Vectors a and c are perpendicular, so both their cosine similarity and dot product are zero.
Key takeaway: Euclidean distance measures proximity, cosine similarity measures directional alignment, and dot product measures alignment weighted by magnitude. For unit-length vectors, dot product and cosine similarity are identical.

title: Transformers
text:
Transformers for natural language processing
The previous section described the transformer layer. This section describes how it is used in natural language processing (NLP) tasks. A typical NLP pipeline starts with a tokenizer that splits the text into words or word fragments. Then each of these tokens is mapped to a learned embedding. These embeddings are passed through a series of transformer layers. We now consider each of these stages in turn.

Sub-word tokenization. a) A passage of text from a nursery rhyme. The tokens are initially just the characters and whitespace (represented by an underscore), and their frequencies are displayed in the table. b) At each iteration, the sub-word tokenizer looks for the most commonly occurring adjacent pair of tokens (in this case, se) and merges them. This creates a new token and decreases the counts for the original tokens s and e. Note that the last character of the first token to be merged cannot be whitespace, which prevents merging across words. c) At the second iteration, the algorithm merges e and the whitespace character_. d) After 23 iterations, the tokens consist of a mix of letters, word fragments, and commonly occurring words. e) If we continue this process indefinitely, the tokens eventually represent the full words. f) Over time, the number of tokens increases as we add word fragments to the letters and then decreases again as we merge these fragments. In a real situation, there would be a very large number of words, and the algorithm would terminate when the vocabulary size (number of tokens) reached a predetermined value. Punctuation and capital letters would also be treated as separate input characters.

title: Transformers
text:
Tokenization
A text processing pipeline begins with a tokenizer. This splits the text into smaller constituent units (tokens) from a vocabulary of possible tokens. In the discussion above, we have implied that these tokens represent words, but there are several difficulties.

Inevitably, some words (e.g., names) will not be in the vocabulary.
It’s unclear how to handle punctuation, but this is important. If a sentence ends in a question mark, we must encode this information.
The vocabulary would need different tokens for versions of the same word with different suffixes (e.g., walk, walks, walked, walking), and there is no way to clarify that these variations are related.

One approach would be to use letters and punctuation marks as the vocabulary, but this would mean splitting text into very small parts and requiring the subsequent network to re-learn the relations between them.
In practice, a compromise between letters and full words is used, and the final vocabulary includes both common words and word fragments from which larger and less frequent words can be composed. The vocabulary is computed using a sub-word tokenizer such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) that greedily merges commonly occurring sub-strings based on their frequency.

Sub-word tokenization.

A passage of text from a nursery rhyme. The tokens are initially just the characters and whitespace (represented by an underscore), and their frequencies are displayed in the table.
At each iteration, the sub-word tokenizer looks for the most commonly occurring adjacent pair of tokens (in this case, se) and merges them. This creates a new token and decreases the counts for the original tokens s and e. Note that the last character of the first token to be merged cannot be whitespace, which prevents merging across words.
At the second iteration, the algorithm merges e and the whitespace character_.
After 23 iterations, the tokens consist of a mix of letters, word fragments, and commonly occurring words.
If we continue this process indefinitely, the tokens eventually represent the full words.
Over time, the number of tokens increases as we add word fragments to the letters and then decreases again as we merge these fragments. In a real situation, there would be a very large number of words, and the algorithm would terminate when the vocabulary size (number of tokens) reached a predetermined value. Punctuation and capital letters would also be treated as separate input characters.

You can visualize how this works using tools like Tiktokenizer (https://tiktokenizer.vercel.app).
For reference, GPT-3 uses 50,257 tokens and GPT-4 uses 100,277 tokens in its vocabulary.

title: Transformers
text:
Embeddings
Each token in the vocabulary \(\mathcal{V}\) is mapped to a unique word embedding, and the embeddings for the whole vocabulary are stored in a matrix \(\Omega_e \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times |\mathcal{V}|}\).
To accomplish this, the \(N\) input tokens are first encoded in the matrix \(T \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times N}\), where the nth column corresponds to the nth token and is a |V|×1 one-hot vector (i.e., a vector where every entry is zero except for the entry corresponding to the token, which is set to one). The input embeddings are computed as \(X= \Omega_e T\), and \(\Omega_e\) is learned like any other network parameter. A typical embedding size D is 1024, and a typical total vocabulary size \(|\mathcal{V}|\) is 30,000, so even before the main network, there are many parameters in \(\Omega_e\) to learn.

The input embedding matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times N}\) contains N embeddings of length D and is created by multiplying a matrix \(\mathbf{\Omega_e}\) containing the embeddings that correspond to the word or sub-word indices. The vocabulary matrix \(\mathbf{\Omega_e}\) is considered a parameter of the model and is learned along with the other parameters. Note that the two embeddings for the word an in \(\mathbf{X}\) are the same.

title: Transformers
text:
Transformer model
Finally, the embedding matrix X representing the text is passed through a series of K transformer layers, called a transformer model. There are three types of transformer models:

Encoder: An encoder transforms the text embeddings into a representation that can support a variety of tasks.
Decoder: A decoder predicts the next token to continue the input text.
Encoder-decoder: Encoder-decoders are used in sequence-to-sequence tasks, where one text string is converted into another (e.g., machine translation).









Architecture

Usually bidirectional self-attention

title: Transformers
text:
Motivation
To motivate the transformer, consider the following passage:

The restaurant refused to serve me a ham sandwich because it only serves vegetarian food. In the end, they just gave me two slices of bread. Their ambiance was just as good as the food and service.

The goal is to design a network to process this text into a representation suitable for downstream tasks.
For example, it might be used to classify the review as positive or negative or to answer questions such as “Does the restaurant serve steak?”.
We can make three immediate observations:

First, the encoded input can be surprisingly large. In this case, each of the 37 words might be represented by an embedding vector of length 1024, so the encoded input would be of length 37×1024 = 37888 even for this small passage.
A more realistically sized body of text might have hundreds or even thousands of words, so fully connected neural networks are impractical.
Second, one of the defining characteristics of NLP problems is that each input (one or more sentences) is of a different length.
It is not even obvious how to apply a fully connected network.
These observations suggest that the network should share parameters across words at different input positions.
Third, language is ambiguous; it is unclear that the pronoun it refers to the restaurant and not to the ham sandwich. To understand the text, the word it should somehow be connected to the word restaurant.
In the parlance of transformers, the former word should pay attention to the latter. This implies that there must be connections between the words and that the strength of these connections will depend on the words themselves. Moreover, these connections need to extend across large text spans. For example, the word their in the last sentence also refers to the restaurant.









Linguistic phenomenon
Example
Connection to learn




Pronoun resolution
The dog chased the cat because it was frightened.
What does it refer to?


Pronoun resolution
Sarah called Emma after she finished work.
Which person finished work?


Subject–verb agreement
The keys to the old cabinet are missing.
Are must agree with keys, not cabinet.


Adjective modification
The old man carried a heavy suitcase.
Which noun does each adjective describe?


Adverb modification
She barely passed the exam.
Barely changes how we interpret passed.


Negation
The movie was not particularly interesting.
Not reverses the evaluation.


Word-sense disambiguation
He sat by the bank and watched the river.
River helps determine the meaning of bank.


Word-sense disambiguation
She deposited money at the bank.
Money and deposited indicate a financial institution.


Long-distance dependency
The book that the professor recommended yesterday was fascinating.
Was relates to book, despite intervening words.


Semantic roles
The chef cooked the fish with a pan.
Pan is an instrument used for cooking.


Semantic roles
The chef cooked the fish with lemon.
Lemon is an ingredient or accompaniment.


Contrast
Although the restaurant was expensive, the food was excellent.
Although signals a contrast between clauses.


Coreference across sentences
John bought a bicycle. He rode it home.
He connects to John; it to bicycle.


Conditional relationships
If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
If establishes a dependency between clauses.



The central teaching point is that a token’s representation should depend not only on the token itself, but also on other relevant tokens in the sequence.

title: Encoder model
text:
In this section, we will discuss encoder models, with a focus on BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) as an example. We will cover the architecture, pre-training, and fine-tuning processes.
BERT is an encoder model that uses a vocabulary of 30,000 tokens. Input tokens are converted to 1024-dimensional word embeddings and passed through 24 transformer layers. Each contains a self-attention mechanism with 16 heads. The queries, keys, and values for each head are of dimension 64 (i.e., the matrices \(\Omega_{vh}, \Omega_{qh}, \Omega_{kh}\) are 64 ×1024).
The dimension of the single hidden layer in the fully connected networks is 4096. The total number of parameters is ∼340 million. When BERT was introduced, this was considered large, but it is now much smaller than state-of-the-art models.

BERT is an encoder model that uses a vocabulary of 30,000 tokens. Input tokens are converted to 1024-dimensional word embeddings and passed through 24 transformer layers. Each contains a self-attention mechanism with 16 heads. The queries, keys, and values for each head are of dimension 64 (i.e., the matrices \(\Omega_{vh}, \Omega_{qh}, \Omega_{kh}\) are 64 ×1024).
The dimension of the single hidden layer in the fully connected networks is 4096. The total number of parameters is ∼340 million. When BERT was introduced, this was considered large, but it is now much smaller than state-of-the-art models. Encoder models like BERT exploit transfer learning (section 9.3.6). During pre- training, the parameters of the transformer architecture are learned using self-supervision from a large corpus of text. The goal here is for the model to learn general information about the statistics of language. In the fine-tuning stage, the resulting network is adapted to solve a particular task using a smaller body of labelled training data.


In the pre-training stage, the network is trained using self-supervision. This allows the use of enormous amounts of data without the need for manual labels. For BERT, the self- supervision task consists of predicting missing words from sentences from a large internet corpus (figure 12.10).1 During training, the maximum input length is 512 tokens, and the batch size is 256. The system is trained for a million steps, corresponding to roughly 50 epochs of the 3.3-billion word corpus. Predicting missing words forces the transformer network to understand some syntax. For example, it might learn that the adjective red is often found before nouns like house or car but never before a verb like shout. It also allows the model to learn superficial common sense about the world. For example, after training, the model will assign a higher probability to the missing word train in the sentence The  pulled into the station than it would to the word peanut. However, the degree of “understanding” this type of model can ever have is limited.

Pre-training for BERT-like encoder. The input tokens (and a special  token denoting the start of the sequence) are converted to word embeddings. Here, these are represented as rows rather than columns, so the box labeled “word embeddings” is XT . These embeddings are passed through a series of transformer layers (orange connections indicate that every token attends to every other token in these layers) to create a set of output embeddings. A small fraction of the input tokens are randomly replaced with a generic  token. In pre-training, the goal is to predict the missing word from the associated output embedding. To this end, the outputs corresponding to the masked tokens are passed through softmax functions, and a multiclass classification loss (section 5.24) is applied to each. This task has the advantage that it uses both the left and right context to predict the missing word but has the disadvantage that it does not make efficient use of data; here, seven tokens need to be processed to add two terms to the loss function.

After pre-training, the encoder is fine-tuned using manually labeled data to solve a particular task. Usually, a linear transformation or a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is appended to the encoder to produce whatever output is required. a) Example text classification task. In this sentiment classification task, the  token embedding is used to predict the probability that the review is positive. b) Example word classification task. In this named entity recognition problem, the embedding for each word is used to predict whether the word corresponds to a person, place, or organization, or is not an entity.



In the fine-tuning stage, the model parameters are adjusted to specialize the network to a particular task. An extra layer is appended onto the transformer network to convert the output vectors to the desired output format. Examples include:
Text classification: In BERT, a special token known as the classification or <cls> token is placed at the start of each string during pre-training. For text classification tasks like sentiment analysis (in which the passage is labeled as having a positive or negative emotional tone), the vector associated with the <cls> token is mapped to a single number and passed through a logistic sigmoid (figure 12.11a). This contributes to a standard binary cross-entropy loss (section 5.4).
Word classification: The goal of named entity recognition is to classify each word as an entity type (e.g., person, place, organization, or no-entity). To this end, each input embedding \(\mathbf{x}_n\) is mapped to an \(E\times 1\) vector where the \(E\) entries correspond to the \(E\) entity types. This is passed through a softmax function to create probabilities for each class, which contribute to a multiclass cross-entropy loss (figure 12.11b).
Text span prediction: In the SQuAD 1.1 question answering task, the question and a passage from Wikipedia containing the answer are concatenated and tokenized. BERT is then used to predict the text span in the passage that contains the answer. Each token maps to two numbers indicating how likely it is that the text span begins and ends at this location. The resulting two sets of numbers are put through two softmax functions. The likelihood of any text span being the answer can be derived by combining the probability of starting and ending at the appropriate places.

Decoder model example: GPT3
This section presents a high-level description of GPT3, an example of a decoder model. The basic architecture is extremely similar to the encoder model and comprises a series of transformer layers that operate on learned word embeddings. However, the goal is different. The encoder aimed to build a representation of the text that could be fine- tuned to solve a variety of more specific NLP tasks. Conversely, the decoder has one purpose: to generate the next token in a sequence. It can generate a coherent text passage by feeding the extended sequence back into the model.

Language modeling
GPT3 is an autoregressive language model. This is easiest to understand with a concrete example. Consider the sentence

It takes great courage to let yourself appear weak.

For simplicity, let’s assume that the tokens are the full words. The probability of the full sentence can be factored as:
\[\begin{eqnarray}
  Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let yourself appear weak}}) &=&\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{takes}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{great}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{courage}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great}})\times\nonumber \\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{to}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage}})\times Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{let}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to}})\times\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{yourself}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let}})\times\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{appear}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let yourself}})\times\nonumber\\
  &&\hspace{-8cm}Pr(\mbox{\textcolor{red}{weak}}|\mbox{\textcolor{red}{It takes great courage to let yourself appear}}).
\end{eqnarray}\]
An autoregressive model predicts the conditional distributions \(Pr(t_n|t_1,...,t_{n-1})\) of each token given all the prior tokens, and hence indirectly computes the joint proba- bility \(Pr(t_1,t_2,...,t_N )\) of all \(N\) tokens:
\[\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq:transformer_autoregressive}
  Pr(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots, t_{N}) = Pr(t_{1})\prod_{n=2}^{N}Pr(t_{n}|t_{1},\ldots, t_{n-1}).
\end{eqnarray}\]
The autoregressive formulation demonstrates the connection between maximizing the joint probability of the tokens and the next token prediction task.


Masked self-attention
To train a decoder, we seek parameters that maximize the log probability of the input text under the autoregressive model (i.e., that maximize the sum of the log conditional probability terms). Ideally, we would pass in the whole sentence and compute all the log probabilities and gradients in the same forward pass rather than doing a forward pass for each token in the sentence. However, if we pass in the full sentence, the term computing log [Pr(great|It takes)] would have access to both the answer great and the right context courage to let yourself appear weak. Hence, the system can cheat rather than learn to predict the following words and won’t train properly.
Fortunately, the tokens only interact in the self-attention layers in a transformer network. Hence, the problem can be resolved by ensuring that the attention to the answer and the right context is zero. This can be achieved by setting the corresponding dot products in the self-attention computation (equation 12.5) to negative infinity before they are passed through the \(\textbf{softmax[•]}\) function. This is known as masked self-attention. The effect is to make the weight of all the upward-angled arrows in figure 12.1 zero.
The entire decoder network operates as follows. The input text is tokenized, and the tokens are converted to embeddings. The embeddings are passed into the transformer network, but now the transformer layers use masked self-attention so that they can only attend to the current and previous tokens. Each of the output embeddings can be thought of as representing a partial sentence, and for each, the goal is to predict the next token in the sequence. Consequently, after the transformer layers, a single linear layer maps each output embedding to the size of the vocabulary, followed by a \(\textbf{softmax[•]}\) function that converts these values to probabilities. During training, we aim to maximize the sum of the log probabilities of the next token in the ground truth sequence at every position using a standard multiclass cross-entropy loss (figure 12.12).


Generating text from a decoder
The autoregressive language model is the first example of a generative model discussed in this book. Since it defines a probability model over text sequences, it can be used to sample new examples of plausible text. To generate from the model, we start with an input sequence of text (which might be just the special  token indicating the beginning of the sequence) and feed this into the network, which then outputs the probabilities over possible subsequent tokens. We can then either pick the most likely token or sample from this probability distribution. The new extended sequence can be fed back into the decoder network to yield the probability distribution over the next token. By repeating this process, we can generate large bodies of text. The computation can be made quite eﬀicient as prior embeddings do not depend on subsequent ones due to the masked self-attention. Hence, much of the earlier computation can be recycled as we generate subsequent tokens.
In practice, many strategies can make the output text more coherent. For example, beam search keeps track of multiple possible sentence completions to find the overall most likely sequence of words (which is not necessarily found by greedily choosing the most likely word at each step). Top-k sampling randomly draws the next word from only the top-K most likely possibilities to prevent the system from accidentally choosing from the long tail of low-probability tokens and leading to an unnecessary linguistic dead end.
