title: The Illustrated Transformer
text:
The Decoder Side
Now that we’ve covered most of the concepts on the encoder side, we basically know how the components of decoders work as well. But let’s take a look at how they work together.
The encoder start by processing the input sequence. The output of the top encoder is then transformed into a set of attention vectors K and V. These are to be used by each decoder in its “encoder-decoder attention” layer which helps the decoder focus on appropriate places in the input sequence:

After finishing the encoding phase, we begin the decoding phase. Each step in the decoding phase outputs an element from the output sequence (the English translation sentence in this case).
The following steps repeat the process until a special symbol is reached indicating the transformer decoder has completed its output. The output of each step is fed to the bottom decoder in the next time step, and the decoders bubble up their decoding results just like the encoders did. And just like we did with the encoder inputs, we embed and add positional encoding to those decoder inputs to indicate the position of each word.

The self attention layers in the decoder operate in a slightly different way than the one in the encoder:
In the decoder, the self-attention layer is only allowed to attend to earlier positions in the output sequence. This is done by masking future positions (setting them to -inf) before the softmax step in the self-attention calculation.
The “Encoder-Decoder Attention” layer works just like multiheaded self-attention, except it creates its Queries matrix from the layer below it, and takes the Keys and Values matrix from the output of the encoder stack.

title: The Illustrated Transformer
section: The Final Linear and Softmax Layer
text:
The Final Linear and Softmax Layer
The decoder stack outputs a vector of floats. How do we turn that into a word? That’s the job of the final Linear layer which is followed by a Softmax Layer.
The Linear layer is a simple fully connected neural network that projects the vector produced by the stack of decoders, into a much, much larger vector called a logits vector.
Let’s assume that our model knows 10,000 unique English words (our model’s “output vocabulary”) that it’s learned from its training dataset. This would make the logits vector 10,000 cells wide – each cell corresponding to the score of a unique word. That is how we interpret the output of the model followed by the Linear layer.
The softmax layer then turns those scores into probabilities (all positive, all add up to 1.0). The cell with the highest probability is chosen, and the word associated with it is produced as the output for this time step.

This figure starts from the bottom with the vector produced as the output of the decoder stack. It is then turned into an output word.

title: The Illustrated Transformer
text:
Recap Of Training
Now that we’ve covered the entire forward-pass process through a trained Transformer, it would be useful to glance at the intuition of training the model.
During training, an untrained model would go through the exact same forward pass. But since we are training it on a labeled training dataset, we can compare its output with the actual correct output.
To visualize this, let’s assume our output vocabulary only contains six words(“a”, “am”, “i”, “thanks”, “student”, and “” (short for ‘end of sentence’)).

The output vocabulary of our model is created in the preprocessing phase before we even begin training.
Once we define our output vocabulary, we can use a vector of the same width to indicate each word in our vocabulary. This also known as one-hot encoding. So for example, we can indicate the word “am” using the following vector:

Example: one-hot encoding of our output vocabulary
Following this recap, let’s discuss the model’s loss function – the metric we are optimizing during the training phase to lead up to a trained and hopefully amazingly accurate model.

title: The Illustrated Transformer
text:
The Loss Function
Say we are training our model. Say it’s our first step in the training phase, and we’re training it on a simple example – translating “merci” into “thanks”.
What this means, is that we want the output to be a probability distribution indicating the word “thanks”. But since this model is not yet trained, that’s unlikely to happen just yet.

Since the model’s parameters (weights) are all initialized randomly, the (untrained) model produces a probability distribution with arbitrary values for each cell/word. We can compare it with the actual output, then tweak all the model’s weights using backpropagation to make the output closer to the desired output.
How do you compare two probability distributions? We simply subtract one from the other. For more details, look at cross-entropy and Kullback–Leibler divergence.
But note that this is an oversimplified example. More realistically, we’ll use a sentence longer than one word. For example – input: “je suis étudiant” and expected output: “i am a student”. What this really means, is that we want our model to successively output probability distributions where:

Each probability distribution is represented by a vector of width vocab_size (6 in our toy example, but more realistically a number like 30,000 or 50,000)
The first probability distribution has the highest probability at the cell associated with the word “i”
The second probability distribution has the highest probability at the cell associated with the word “am”
And so on, until the fifth output distribution indicates ‘<end of sentence>’ symbol, which also has a cell associated with it from the 10,000 element vocabulary.


The targeted probability distributions we’ll train our model against in the training example for one sample sentence.
After training the model for enough time on a large enough dataset, we would hope the produced probability distributions would look like this:

Hopefully upon training, the model would output the right translation we expect. Of course it’s no real indication if this phrase was part of the training dataset (see: cross validation). Notice that every position gets a little bit of probability even if it’s unlikely to be the output of that time step – that’s a very useful property of softmax which helps the training process.
Now, because the model produces the outputs one at a time, we can assume that the model is selecting the word with the highest probability from that probability distribution and throwing away the rest. That’s one way to do it (called greedy decoding). Another way to do it would be to hold on to, say, the top two words (say, ‘I’ and ‘a’ for example), then in the next step, run the model twice: once assuming the first output position was the word ‘I’, and another time assuming the first output position was the word ‘a’, and whichever version produced less error considering both positions #1 and #2 is kept. We repeat this for positions #2 and #3…etc. This method is called “beam search”, where in our example, beam_size was two (meaning that at all times, two partial hypotheses (unfinished translations) are kept in memory), and top_beams is also two (meaning we’ll return two translations). These are both hyperparameters that you can experiment with.

title: Encoder model
text:
Pre-training


Pre-training for BERT-like encoder. The input tokens (and a special  token denoting the start of the sequence) are converted to word embeddings.
Here, these are represented as rows rather than columns, so the box labeled “word embeddings” is \(\mathbf{X}^T\) . These embeddings are passed through a series of transformer layers (orange connections indicate that every token attends to every other token in these layers) to create a set of output embeddings.
A small fraction of the input tokens are randomly replaced with a generic  token.
In pre-training, the goal is to predict the missing word from the associated output embedding.
To this end, the outputs corresponding to the masked tokens are passed through softmax functions, and a multiclass classification loss is applied to each.
This task has the advantage that it uses both the left and right context to predict the missing word but has the disadvantage that it does not make efficient use of data; here, seven tokens need to be processed to add two terms to the loss function.
In the pre-training stage, the network is trained using self-supervision. This allows the use of enormous amounts of data without the need for manual labels.
For BERT, the self-supervision task consists of predicting missing words from sentences from a large internet corpus (figure 12.10).
During training, the maximum input length is 512 tokens, and the batch size is 256.
The system is trained for a million steps, corresponding to roughly 50 epochs of the 3.3-billion word corpus.
Predicting missing words forces the transformer network to understand some syntax.
For example, it might learn that the adjective red is often found before nouns like house or car but never before a verb like shout.
It also allows the model to learn superficial common sense about the world. For example, after training, the model will assign a higher probability to the missing word train in the sentence The  pulled into the station than it would to the word peanut. However, the degree of “understanding” this type of model can ever have is limited.

Masked Language Modeling
Masked language modeling (MLM) is a pre-training objective where certain tokens in the input sequence are randomly masked, and the model is trained to predict these masked tokens based on their surrounding context.
During pre-training, the parameters of the transformer encoder are learned through self-supervised learning on a large corpus of text. The objective is to predict masked tokens using their surrounding context, allowing the model to learn the statistical patterns and relationships within language.
The text is first tokenized using a subword tokenization algorithm (such as BPE or WordPiece) and converted into token IDs. These token IDs are organized into fixed- or variable-length input sequences. For each sequence, 15% of token positions are randomly selected for prediction. In the original BERT approach, 80% of these selected tokens are replaced with the special [MASK] token ID, 10% with a random token ID, and 10% are left unchanged.
The [MASK] token has its own learnable embedding vector in the embedding matrix. The modified sequence is passed through the transformer encoder, which produces a contextualized representation for every token position. At each selected position, the model uses this representation to predict the original token ID, which serves as the training label. The prediction error is used to update the model’s parameters through backpropagation.
The goal here is for the model to learn general information about the statistics of language.
In the fine-tuning stage, the resulting network is adapted to solve a particular task using a smaller body of labelled training data.


Internet-scale data

Common Crawl
Common Crawl is a non-profit organization that crawls the web and freely provides its archives and datasets to the public. It is one of the largest and most comprehensive web crawls available. It has been crawling the web since 2008 and has petabytes (thousands of terabytes) of data.
The code and data are open source and free to use for anyone. Code can be accessed at https://github.com/commoncrawl and the data can be accessed at https://data.commoncrawl.org/.
HuggingFace is a company and open-source community that provides tools and libraries for natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. They are most well-known for:

Transformers library, which provides pre-trained models for various NLP tasks.
Data Sharing a platform for sharing and discovering datasets, models, and other resources related to NLP.
Model Hub, which hosts thousands of pre-trained models for various NLP tasks.




FineWeb
Fineweb is a dataset created by Hugging Face that consists of cleaned and filtered web pages from Common Crawl. It is derived from 96 Common Crawl snapshots. Extensive filtering (boilerplate removal, quality heuristics), deduplication, and cleaning to produce higher-quality web text than raw Common Crawl for FineWeb. It is designed to be used for training large language models. The dataset contains over 1.2 billion web pages, making it one of the largest datasets available for this purpose.
Once cleaned, the data still needs to be compressed into something usable. Instead of feeding raw text into the model, it gets converted into tokens: a structured, numerical representation.



Demo: Reproducing OpenAI’s GPT-2
GPT-2, released by OpenAI in 2019, was an early example of a transformer-based LLM.
Here’s what it looked like:

1.6 billion parameters
1024-token context length
Trained on ~100 billion tokens
The original GPT-2 training cost was $40,000.

Since then, efficiency has improved dramatically. Andrej Karpathy managed to reproduce GPT-2 using llm.c for just $672. With optimized pipelines, training costs could drop even further to around $100 .
Why is it so much cheaper now?

Better pre-training data extraction techniques → Cleaner datasets mean models learn faster.
Stronger hardware and optimized software → Less computation needed for the same results.



Open Base Models
The models under discussion do not strictly follow the Open Source Initiative (OSI) definitions of open-source AI ([OSI AI Definition](https://opensource.org/ai)). Instead, we use the term open base models to describe models where the weights are publicly accessible, but training data and full reproducibility may not be provided.
Some companies train massive language models (LMs) and release the base models for free. A base model is essentially a raw, pre-trained LM—it still requires fine-tuning or alignment to be practically useful.

Base models are trained on unfiltered internet-scale data, meaning they generate raw completions but lack alignment with human intent.
OpenAI released GPT-2, an open-weight and source-available model, but not fully open-source under OSI’s definition since its training data was not released.
Meta released Llama 3.1 (405B parameters), an open-weight but not open-source model.

To release a base model, two key components are required:

Inference code → Defines the steps the model follows to generate text. Typically written in Python.
Model weights → The billions of parameters that encode the model’s knowledge. ## The ‘Psychology’ of Base Models


Base models can be thoughts of as token-level internet document simulators.
Every run produces a slightly different output (stochastic behavior).
They can regurgitate parts of their training data.
The parameters are like a lossy zip file of internet knowledge.
You can already use them for applications like:

Translation → Using in-context examples.
Basic assistants → Prompting them in a structured way.


Want to experiment with one? Try the Llama 3 (405B base model) here.
At its core, a base model is just an expensive autocomplete. It still needs fine-tuning.

title: Encoder model
text:
Supervised Fine-tuning


After pre-training, the encoder is fine-tuned using manually labeled data to solve a particular task. Usually, a linear transformation or a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is appended to the encoder to produce whatever output is required.

Example text classification task. In this sentiment classification task, the  token embedding is used to predict the probability that the review is positive.
Example word classification task. In this named entity recognition problem, the embedding for each word is used to predict whether the word corresponds to a person, place, or organization, or is not an entity.

In the fine-tuning stage, the model parameters are adjusted to specialize the network to a particular task. An extra layer is appended onto the transformer network to convert the output vectors to the desired output format. Examples include:
Text classification: In BERT, a special token known as the classification or <cls> token is placed at the start of each string during pre-training. For text classification tasks like sentiment analysis (in which the passage is labeled as having a positive or negative emotional tone), the vector associated with the <cls> token is mapped to a single number and passed through a logistic sigmoid (figure 12.11a). This contributes to a standard binary cross-entropy loss (section 5.4).
Word classification: The goal of named entity recognition is to classify each word as an entity type (e.g., person, place, organization, or no-entity). To this end, each input embedding \(\mathbf{x}_n\) is mapped to an \(E\times 1\) vector where the \(E\) entries correspond to the \(E\) entity types. This is passed through a softmax function to create probabilities for each class, which contribute to a multiclass cross-entropy loss (figure 12.11b).
Text span prediction: In the SQuAD 1.1 question answering task, the question and a passage from Wikipedia containing the answer are concatenated and tokenized. BERT is then used to predict the text span in the passage that contains the answer. Each token maps to two numbers indicating how likely it is that the text span begins and ends at this location. The resulting two sets of numbers are put through two softmax functions. The likelihood of any text span being the answer can be derived by combining the probability of starting and ending at the appropriate places.

title: Encoder model
text:
1.2. Tokenization
You can visualize how this works using tools like Tiktokenizer (https://tiktokenizer.vercel.app).
LLMs don’t operate directly on raw text. Instead: 1. Text → tokenizer → tokens (subword units). 2. Tokens → mapped to integers (IDs in a fixed vocabulary). 3. These IDs are fed into the model for training or inference.
For reference, GPT-3 uses 50,257 tokens and GPT-4 uses 100,277 tokens in its vocabulary.


You can see a production-grade LLM architecture example here.

title: Encoder model
text:
1.3. Embeddings
After BPE, input text is split into subword tokens. Each token is now just an integer ID (index in the vocabulary).
We need to convert these integer IDs into a numerical format that the model can understand. This is where embeddings come in.
An embedding is a dense vector representation of a token in a continuous vector space. Each token is mapped to a high-dimensional vector (e.g., 768, 1024, or even 2048 dimensions). These vectors capture semantic meaning, so similar tokens have similar vectors.
For example, the words “king” and “queen” might have embeddings that are close together in the vector space, while “king” and “car” would be far apart.
Each token ID is then mapped to a dense vector using an embedding matrix E of size [Vocab_size × Embedding_dim]. Suppose Vocab_size = 30,000 and Embedding_dim = 512, then E is a 30,000 × 512 matrix.
If token ID = 421, you take the 421st row of E.
Embeddings are learned during training. The model starts with random vectors for each token and adjusts them based on the context in which the tokens appear. Over time, the embeddings capture relationships between words, such as synonyms, analogies, and more.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

vocab_size = 30000
embed_dim = 512

embedding_layer = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim)

# Example: two BPE tokens
token_ids = torch.tensor([421, 88])  # "jouer" split into two tokens
embeddings = embedding_layer(token_ids)

print(embeddings.shape)  # torch.Size([2, 512])

title: Encoder model
text:
1.3. Neural Network Training
Once the data is tokenized, it’s fed into the neural network. More specifically, a Transformer architecture, which is particularly good at handling sequential data like text.


Here’s how that process works:

The model takes in a context window, a set number of tokens (e.g., 8,000 for some models, up to 128k for GPT-4).
It predicts the next token based on the patterns it has learned.
The weights in the model are adjusted using backpropagation to reduce errors.
Over time, the model learns to make better predictions.

A longer context window means the model can “remember” more from the input, but it also increases computational cost.
Neural Network Internals

Inside the model, billions of parameters interact with the input tokens to generate a probability distribution for the next token.

This process is defined by complex mathematical equations optimized for efficiency.
Model architectures are designed to balance speed, accuracy, and parallelization.
You can see a production-grade LLM architecture example here.

title: Encoder model
text:
1.4. Inference

LLMs don’t generate deterministic outputs, they are stochastic. This means the output varies slightly every time you run the model.

The model doesn’t just repeat what it was trained on, it generates responses based on probabilities.
In some cases, the response will match something in the training data exactly, but most of the time, it will generate something new that follows similar patterns.

This randomness is why LLMs can be creative, but also why they sometimes hallucinate incorrect information.

title: Encoder model
text:
2.1. Conversations Data
Once the base model is trained on internet data, the next step is post-training. This is where we replace the internet dataset with human/assistant conversations to make the model more conversational and useful.

Pre-training takes months, but post-training is much faster. It can take as little as a few hours.
The model’s algorithm stays the same, we’re just fine-tuning the existing parameters.

To teach a model how to handle back-and-forth conversations, we use chat templates. These define the structure of a conversation and let the model know which part is user input and which part is an assistant response. You can read more about them here.
Example template:
<|im_start|>system<|im_sep|>You are a helpful assistant<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user<|im_sep|>What is 4 + 4?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant<|im_sep|>4 + 4 = 8<|im_end|>

<|im_start|> and <|im_end|> are special tokens that help structure conversations.
The model didn’t see these new tokens during pre-training, they’re introduced during post-training.
OpenAI has discussed fine-tuning LLMs for conversation in the InstructGPT paper.

To visualize this, go to tiktokenizer.
One such post-training dataset is OASST1. Early post-training datasets were hand-curated by humans. Now, models like UltraChat can generate synthetic conversations, allowing models to improve without as much human input. You can visualize these mostly synthetic datasets here.

title: Encoder model
text:
2.2. Hallucinations, Tool Use, and Memory
One major issue with LLMs is hallucination, where the model confidently generates incorrect or made-up information.
Why does this happen?

During post-training, models learn that they must always give an answer.
Even if the question doesn’t make sense, the model tries to generate a response instead of saying, “I don’t know.”

How Meta Deals with Hallucinations
Meta’s research on factuality (from their Llama 3 paper) describes a way to improve this:

Extract a snippet of training data.
Generate a factual question about it using Llama 3.
Have Llama 3 generate an answer.
Score the response against the original data.
If incorrect, train the model to recognize and refuse incorrect responses.

Essentially, this process teaches models to recognize their own knowledge limits.

title: Encoder model
text:
2.3. Using Tools to Reduce Hallucinations
One way to fix hallucinations is to train models to use tools when they don’t know the answer. This approach follows the pattern:
<|im_start|>user<|im_sep|>Who is Orson Kovacs?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant<|im_sep|><SEARCH_START>Who is Orson Kovacs?<SEARCH_END><|im_end|>

[...search results...]

<|im_start|>assistant<|im_sep|>Orson Kovacs is ....<|im_end|>
With repeated training, models learn that if they don’t know something, they should look it up instead of making things up.
“Vague Recollection” vs. “Working Memory”

Model parameters store vague recollections (like remembering something from a month ago).
Context tokens function as working memory, giving models access to fresh information.

This is why retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) works so well: if the model has direct access to relevant documents, it doesn’t need to guess.

title: Encoder model
text:
2.4. Knowledge of Self
If you prompt an untuned base model about who it is, it will likely hallucinate. For example, a non-OpenAI model might still say it was created by OpenAI simply because most internet data links AI models to OpenAI.
How to Fix This

Hardcode self-identity into training data → Example: Olmo-2 dataset.
Use system messages → At the start of every conversation, include a reminder of its identity.

By default, LLMs have no real knowledge of themselves. Without specific training, they default to generic AI responses.

title: Encoder model
text:
2.5. Models Need Tokens to Think
LLMs don’t reason like humans. They generate tokens sequentially, meaning they need structured generation to think properly.
Example: Bad vs. Good Model Output
Bad Model Output:
Human: Emily buys 3 apples and 2 oranges. Each orange costs $2. The total cost of all the fruit is $13. What is the cost of apples? Assistant: The answer is $3.
The model jumps to the answer without breaking it down.
Good Model Output:
Human: Emily buys 3 apples and 2 oranges. Each orange costs $2. The total cost of all the fruit is $13. What is the cost of apples? Assistant: The total cost of the oranges is $4. 13 - 4 = 9, so the cost of the 3 apples is $9. 9/3 = 3, so each apple costs $3.
Here, the model works through the reasoning step-by-step.
Why This Matters

If a model jumps straight to an answer, it might just be guessing.
If it walks through the solution step-by-step, it’s more reliable.
The model breaks down the problem into smaller steps. Since there are finite layers in the model, one token output cannot be processed indefinitely. Breaking down the problem into smaller steps allows the model to process the problem in a way that is more likely to yield the correct answer.

For math and logic tasks, it’s best to ask the model to use external tools rather than relying on its own reasoning.

title: Encoder model
text:
Post-Training: Supervised Fine-tuning
So far, we’ve looked at base models, which are just pre-trained text generators. But to make an actual assistant, you need post-training.
Base models hallucinate a lot → They generate text, but it’s not always useful.
Post-training fixes this by fine-tuning the model to respond better.
The good news? Post-training is way cheaper than pre-training (e.g., months vs. hours).

This is passed through a softmax function to create probabilities for each class, which contribute to a multiclass cross-entropy loss (figure 12.11b).
Text span prediction: In the SQuAD 1.1 question answering task, the question and a passage from Wikipedia containing the answer are concatenated and tokenized. BERT is then used to predict the text span in the passage that contains the answer. Each token maps to two numbers indicating how likely it is that the text span begins and ends at this location. The resulting two sets of numbers are put through two softmax functions. The likelihood of any text span being the answer can be derived by combining the probability of starting and ending at the appropriate places.


You can see a production-grade LLM architecture example here.


Conversations Data
Once the base model is trained on internet data, the next step is post-training. This is where we replace the internet dataset with human/assistant conversations to make the model more conversational and useful.

Pre-training takes months, but post-training is much faster. It can take as little as a few hours.
The model’s algorithm stays the same, we’re just fine-tuning the existing parameters.

To teach a model how to handle back-and-forth conversations, we use chat templates. These define the structure of a conversation and let the model know which part is user input and which part is an assistant response. You can read more about them here.
Example template:
<|im_start|>system<|im_sep|>You are a helpful assistant<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user<|im_sep|>What is 4 + 4?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant<|im_sep|>4 + 4 = 8<|im_end|>

<|im_start|> and <|im_end|> are special tokens that help structure conversations.
The model didn’t see these new tokens during pre-training, they’re introduced during post-training.
OpenAI has discussed fine-tuning LLMs for conversation in the InstructGPT paper.

To visualize this, go to tiktokenizer.
One such post-training dataset is OASST1. Early post-training datasets were hand-curated by humans. Now, models like UltraChat can generate synthetic conversations, allowing models to improve without as much human input. You can visualize these mostly synthetic datasets here.


Hallucinations, Tool Use, and Memory
One major issue with LLMs is hallucination, where the model confidently generates incorrect or made-up information.
Why does this happen?

During post-training, models learn that they must always give an answer.
Even if the question doesn’t make sense, the model tries to generate a response instead of saying, “I don’t know.”

How Meta Deals with Hallucinations
Meta’s research on factuality (from their Llama 3 paper) describes a way to improve this:

Extract a snippet of training data.
Generate a factual question about it using Llama 3.
Have Llama 3 generate an answer.
Score the response against the original data.
If incorrect, train the model to recognize and refuse incorrect responses.

Essentially, this process teaches models to recognize their own knowledge limits.


Using Tools to Reduce Hallucinations
One way to fix hallucinations is to train models to use tools when they don’t know the answer. This approach follows the pattern:
<|im_start|>user<|im_sep|>Who is Orson Kovacs?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant<|im_sep|><SEARCH_START>Who is Orson Kovacs?<SEARCH_END><|im_end|>

[...search results...]

<|im_start|>assistant<|im_sep|>Orson Kovacs is ....<|im_end|>
With repeated training, models learn that if they don’t know something, they should look it up instead of making things up.
“Vague Recollection” vs. “Working Memory”

Model parameters store vague recollections (like remembering something from a month ago).
Context tokens function as working memory, giving models access to fresh information.

This is why retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) works so well: if the model has direct access to relevant documents, it doesn’t need to guess.


Knowledge of Self
If you prompt an untuned base model about who it is, it will likely hallucinate. For example, a non-OpenAI model might still say it was created by OpenAI simply because most internet data links AI models to OpenAI.
How to Fix This

Hardcode self-identity into training data → Example: Olmo-2 dataset.
Use system messages → At the start of every conversation, include a reminder of its identity.

By default, LLMs have no real knowledge of themselves. Without specific training, they default to generic AI responses.

title: Dot-product self-attention
text:
In machine learning, data points are often represented as vectors in a high-dimensional space. For example, word embeddings represent words as vectors, with semantically related words often occupying nearby regions of the embedding space. To compare two vectors, we need a way to measure how similar they are.
Three commonly used measures are Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, and dot product. Although closely related mathematically, they capture different aspects of the relationship between vectors.


Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between two points in space.
For two vectors () and ():
[ d(,)= ]
A smaller distance indicates that the vectors are closer together. Euclidean distance considers both the direction and magnitude of the vectors.



Cosine similarity measures the angle between two nonzero vectors, regardless of their magnitudes.
[ ()= ]

1: Vectors point in the same direction.
0: Vectors are perpendicular.
−1: Vectors point in opposite directions.

For example, the vectors ([1,2]) and ([10,20]) have a cosine similarity of 1, even though they are far apart in Euclidean distance.
Cosine similarity is particularly useful when the direction of a vector is more important than its magnitude.



The dot product of two vectors is calculated by multiplying corresponding components and summing the results:
[ =_{i=1}^{d}a_i b_i ]
Geometrically, the dot product can also be expressed as:
[ =||||() ]
This reveals an important relationship: the dot product combines angular alignment (cosine similarity) with vector magnitudes.
Two vectors have a large positive dot product when they point in similar directions and have large magnitudes. Their dot product is zero when they are perpendicular and negative when they point in opposing directions.
Unlike cosine similarity, the dot product is not normalized. Consequently, two vectors can have a high dot product because of their magnitudes, even if they are not especially well aligned.



Consider three vectors:
[ =[1,2],=[2,4],=[-2,1] ]



Comparison

Cosine Similarity

Vectors a and b point in exactly the same direction, giving them a cosine similarity of 1, but they have different magnitudes and therefore a nonzero Euclidean distance. Vectors a and c are perpendicular, so both their cosine similarity and dot product are zero.



In transformer self-attention, the similarity between query and key vectors is measured using their dot product.
[ (Q,K,V)= ()V ]
The dot product allows the model to learn how strongly a query and key should interact, based on both their alignment and their learned magnitudes.
Unlike cosine similarity, which explicitly normalizes vectors, dot-product attention allows vector magnitudes to influence attention scores. The division by () helps control the scale of these scores as the dimensionality increases.
Key takeaway: Euclidean distance measures proximity, cosine similarity measures directional alignment, and dot product measures alignment weighted by magnitude. For unit-length vectors, dot product and cosine similarity are identical.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Layer Normalization (LayerNorm)
Suppose a token has a four-dimensional embedding:
\[ x=[2,4,6,8] \]
Its mean is:
\[ \mu=\frac{2+4+6+8}{4}=5 \]
Its standard deviation is:
\[ \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{(2-5)^2+(4-5)^2+(6-5)^2+(8-5)^2}{4}}=\sqrt{5} \]
LayerNorm first standardizes the vector:
\[ \hat{x}=\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}} \]
Ignoring the tiny \(\) for simplicity:
\[ \hat{x}\approx[-1.34,-0.45,0.45,1.34] \]
Now the vector has approximately:

Mean = 0
Standard deviation = 1

But LayerNorm doesn’t stop there. It also learns a scale and shift for each dimension:
\[ \boxed{y=\gamma\odot\hat{x}+\beta} \]
Here, \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learnable parameters, each with four elements in this example. They allow the network to adjust the standardized representation.
What exactly gets normalized in a transformer?
Suppose the input has shape:
\[ (\text{batch},\text{tokens},\text{embedding dimensions}) =(32,64,128) \]
LayerNorm normalizes each token’s 128-dimensional vector independently.
LayerNorm operates across embedding dimensions
Each row is normalized separately. The same learned γ and β parameters are shared across token positions.
This is different from Batch Normalization, which uses statistics across examples in a batch.
Where does LayerNorm appear in our transformer?
Recall our implementation:
attention_output = self.attention(x)
x = self.norm1(x + attention_output)
ff_output = self.feedforward(x)
x = self.norm2(x + ff_output)
The first LayerNorm normalizes the result of the attention block plus its residual connection.
The second normalizes the result of the feed-forward block plus its residual connection.
This is called a Post-LayerNorm transformer, because normalization happens after each residual addition. Many modern transformer architectures instead use Pre-LayerNorm, which normalizes before each sublayer.
PyTorch implementation
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
x = torch.tensor([[2., 4., 6., 8.]])
norm = nn.LayerNorm(4)
y = norm(x)
print(y)
The important detail is that nn.LayerNorm(4) creates 8 learnable parameters:

Four scale parameters (\(\))
Four shift parameters (\(\))

For our transformer with d_model=128, each LayerNorm has 256 learnable parameters.
Why do we need it?
During training, the outputs of attention and feed-forward layers can change in magnitude as their parameters are updated. LayerNorm helps keep the scale of representations more controlled, making optimization more stable.
It also helps gradients propagate through deep transformer networks.
One important distinction: LayerNorm does not make all token embeddings identical or erase their contextual information. It normalizes each vector’s mean and variance, while preserving differences in the relative values of its dimensions.
In short, self-attention determines what information each token receives; LayerNorm helps keep the resulting representations numerically well-behaved.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Residual connections
Residual connections are a key component of transformer layers. They allow the network to retain information from earlier layers by adding the input of a layer to its output. This helps mitigate the vanishing gradient problem and enables the training of very deep networks.
Mathematically, if a layer implements a function \(F(\mathbf{X})\), the residual connection produces an output \(\mathbf{X} + F(\mathbf{X})\). In transformers, both the multi-head self-attention and the feed-forward sub-layers use residual connections.

import math
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F


# Configuration
torch.manual_seed(42)

BATCH_SIZE      = 32
CONTEXT_LENGTH  = 64
EMBEDDING_DIM   = 64
LEARNING_RATE   = 1e-3
TRAINING_STEPS  = 2000
EVAL_INTERVAL   = 100
EVAL_BATCHES    = 20

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    DEVICE = "cuda"
elif torch.backends.mps.is_available():
    DEVICE = "mps"
else:
    DEVICE = "cpu"


# Data preparation
text = Path("input.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
characters = sorted(set(text))
vocabulary_size = len(characters)

character_to_id = {character: i for i, character in enumerate(characters)}
id_to_character = {i: character for character, i in character_to_id.items()}


def encode(text):
    return [character_to_id[character] for character in text]

def decode(ids):
    return "".join(id_to_character[i] for i in ids)


data = torch.tensor(encode(text), dtype=torch.long)
split_index = int(0.9 * len(data))

datasets = {
    "train": data[:split_index],
    "validation": data[split_index:],
}

if vocabulary_size < 2:
    raise ValueError("The corpus must contain at least two characters.")

for name, dataset in datasets.items():
    if len(dataset) <= CONTEXT_LENGTH:
        raise ValueError(
            f"The {name} split needs more than "
            f"{CONTEXT_LENGTH} characters."
        )




def get_batch(split):
    """Return inputs and next-character targets, both shaped (B, T)."""
    dataset = datasets[split]

    starts = torch.randint(
        len(dataset) - CONTEXT_LENGTH,
        (BATCH_SIZE,),
    )

    inputs = torch.stack([
        dataset[start:start + CONTEXT_LENGTH]
        for start in starts
    ])

    targets = torch.stack([
        dataset[start + 1:start + CONTEXT_LENGTH + 1]
        for start in starts
    ])

    return inputs.to(DEVICE), targets.to(DEVICE)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """One attention head, implemented explicitly."""

    def __init__(self, embedding_dim, context_length):
        super().__init__()

        self.query              = nn.Linear(embedding_dim, embedding_dim, bias=False)
        self.key                = nn.Linear(embedding_dim, embedding_dim, bias=False)
        self.value              = nn.Linear(embedding_dim, embedding_dim, bias=False)
        self.output_projection  = nn.Linear(embedding_dim, embedding_dim)

        # True marks a permitted connection, including the diagonal.
        allowed = torch.ones(context_length, context_length, dtype=torch.bool).tril()

        self.register_buffer("allowed", allowed)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (B, T, C)
        _, length, channels = x.shape

        queries = self.query(x)  # (B, T, C)
        keys    = self.key(x)       # (B, T, C)
        values  = self.value(x)   # (B, T, C)

        # Each query is compared with every key in its sequence.
        scores = queries @ keys.transpose(-2, -1)  # (B, T, T)
        scores = scores / math.sqrt(channels)

        # Mask future positions BEFORE softmax.
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~self.allowed[:length, :length], float("-inf"),)

        weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)  # (B, T, T)
        attended = weights @ values         # (B, T, C)

        return self.output_projection(attended), weights


class AttentionLanguageModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocabulary_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.token_embedding    = nn.Embedding(vocabulary_size, EMBEDDING_DIM)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(CONTEXT_LENGTH, EMBEDDING_DIM)
        self.attention_norm     = nn.LayerNorm(EMBEDDING_DIM)
        self.attention          = CausalSelfAttention(EMBEDDING_DIM, CONTEXT_LENGTH)
        self.final_norm         = nn.LayerNorm(EMBEDDING_DIM)
        self.language_head      = nn.Linear(EMBEDDING_DIM, vocabulary_size)

    def forward(self, token_ids, targets=None):
        # token_ids: (B, T)
        _, length = token_ids.shape

        if length > CONTEXT_LENGTH:
            raise ValueError("Input exceeds the context length.")

        positions = torch.arange(length, device=token_ids.device)

        x = (self.token_embedding(token_ids) + self.position_embedding(positions))  # (B, T, C)

        update, weights = self.attention(self.attention_norm(x))
        x = x + update  # Residual connection

        logits = self.language_head(self.final_norm(x))  # (B, T, vocabulary_size)

        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, vocabulary_size),targets.reshape(-1),)

        return logits, loss, weights

    @torch.no_grad()
    def generate(self, token_ids, new_characters=300):
        was_training = self.training
        self.eval()

        for _ in range(new_characters):
            # Retain only the supported context window.
            context = token_ids[:, -CONTEXT_LENGTH:]
            logits, _, _ = self(context)

            # The final position predicts the next character.
            probabilities = F.softmax(
                logits[:, -1, :], dim=-1
            )
            next_id = torch.multinomial(
                probabilities, num_samples=1
            )

            token_ids = torch.cat(
                [token_ids, next_id], dim=1
            )

        self.train(was_training)
        return token_ids


@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_losses(model):
    was_training = model.training
    model.eval()
    results = {}

    for split in datasets:
        losses = []

        for _ in range(EVAL_BATCHES):
            inputs, targets = get_batch(split)
            _, loss, _ = model(inputs, targets)
            losses.append(loss.item())

        results[split] = sum(losses) / len(losses)

    model.train(was_training)
    return results


@torch.no_grad()
def check_causality(model):
    """Changing future inputs must not change earlier logits."""
    was_training = model.training
    model.eval()

    inputs, _ = get_batch("validation")
    changed = inputs.clone()
    cutoff = CONTEXT_LENGTH // 2

    changed[:, cutoff:] = (
        changed[:, cutoff:] + 1
    ) % vocabulary_size

    original_logits, _, weights = model(inputs)
    changed_logits, _, _ = model(changed)

    torch.testing.assert_close(
        original_logits[:, :cutoff],
        changed_logits[:, :cutoff],
        atol=1e-5,
        rtol=1e-5,
    )

    # Every attention weight above the diagonal must be zero.
    assert torch.count_nonzero(
        torch.triu(weights, diagonal=1)
    ).item() == 0

    model.train(was_training)
    print("Causality check passed.")

from collections import Counter


def merge_pair(tokens, pair, new_id):
    """Replace non-overlapping occurrences of pair with new_id."""
    result = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(tokens):
        if (i + 1 < len(tokens) and (tokens[i], tokens[i + 1]) == pair):
            result.append(new_id)
            i += 2
        else:
            result.append(tokens[i])
            i += 1

    return result


def byte_pair_encoding(encoded, vocab_size):
    encoded = list(encoded)

    if not encoded:
        return encoded

    # Track the vocabulary separately from tokens still in the sequence.
    current_vocab_size = len(set(encoded))
    new_id = max(encoded) + 1

    while current_vocab_size < vocab_size:
        # print("Current vocabulary size:", current_vocab_size,"Target vocabulary size:", vocab_size,)

        pairs = Counter(zip(encoded, encoded[1:]))

        if not pairs:
            break  # No adjacent tokens remain to merge.

        pair, count = pairs.most_common(1)[0]
        # print("Merging:", pair, "Count:", count, "New ID:", new_id)

        encoded = merge_pair(encoded, pair, new_id)

        new_id += 1
        current_vocab_size += 1

    return encoded

Note that transforms.Compose combines image transformations into a sequence and applies them in the order listed whenever an image is loaded. In this notebook, it converts images into PyTorch tensors using ToTensor() and normalizes each color channel using Normalize(). For data augmentation, we add transformations such as random crops and horizontal flips before ToTensor(). These random transformations can produce a different version of an image each time it is loaded during training. For validation and testing, we use only conversion and normalization so that evaluation images are not randomly altered.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from PIL import Image
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from torchvision import transforms

images = ds["train"]["img"]
labels = ds["train"]["fine_label"]

# Reuse the existing stratified split.
X_train = train_ds["img"]
y_train = train_ds["fine_label"]

X_valid = valid_ds["img"]
y_valid = valid_ds["fine_label"]

X_test = test_ds["img"]
y_test = test_ds["fine_label"]


class MyDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.features = X
        self.labels = y
        self.transform = transforms.Compose([
            transforms.ToTensor(),
            transforms.Normalize(
                (0.5071, 0.4867, 0.4408),
                (0.2675, 0.2565, 0.2761)
            ),
        ])

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        image = self.features[index]

        # Handles PIL images or original uint8 image arrays.
        if not isinstance(image, Image.Image):
            image = Image.fromarray(np.asarray(image))

        image = self.transform(image.convert("RGB"))
        label = torch.tensor(int(self.labels[index]), dtype=torch.long)
        return image, label

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.features)


train_dataset = MyDataset(X_train, y_train)
val_dataset = MyDataset(X_valid, y_valid)

train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True
)
val_loader = DataLoader(
    val_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=False
)

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    device = torch.device("cuda")
elif torch.backends.mps.is_available():
    device = torch.device("mps")
else:
    device = torch.device("cpu")



model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(512, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 100),
).to(device)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

num_epochs = 25

train_loss_history = []
val_loss_history = []

train_accuracy_history = []
val_accuracy_history = []

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    train_loss_sum = 0.0
    train_correct = 0
    train_count = 0

    for inputs, targets in train_loader:
        inputs = inputs.to(device)
        targets = targets.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        batch_size = targets.size(0)
        train_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
        train_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
        train_count += batch_size

    model.eval()
    val_loss_sum = 0.0
    val_correct = 0
    val_count = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, targets in val_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            targets = targets.to(device)

            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

            batch_size = targets.size(0)
            val_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
            val_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
            val_count += batch_size

    train_loss_history.append(train_loss_sum / train_count)
    val_loss_history.append(val_loss_sum / val_count)

    print(

        f"Val loss: {val_loss_sum / val_count:.4f} | "
        f"Val accuracy: {val_correct / val_count:.2%}"
    )

    train_accuracy_history.append(train_correct / train_count)
    val_accuracy_history.append(val_correct / val_count)

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(512, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 100),
).to(device)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

num_epochs = 25

train_with_reg_loss_history = []
val_with_reg_loss_history = []

train_with_reg_accuracy_history = []
val_with_reg_accuracy_history = []

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    train_loss_sum = 0.0
    train_correct = 0
    train_count = 0

    for inputs, targets in train_loader:
        inputs = inputs.to(device)
        targets = targets.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

        # Add the weight penalty
        my_lambd = 1e-5
        penalty = sum([(param.sum() ** 2) for param in model.parameters()])
        loss = loss + (my_lambd * penalty)

        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        batch_size = targets.size(0)
        train_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
        train_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
        train_count += batch_size

    model.eval()
    val_loss_sum = 0.0
    val_correct = 0
    val_count = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, targets in val_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            targets = targets.to(device)

            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

            batch_size = targets.size(0)
            val_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
            val_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
            val_count += batch_size

    train_with_reg_loss_history.append(train_loss_sum / train_count)
    val_with_reg_loss_history.append(val_loss_sum / val_count)

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch + 1}/{num_epochs} | "
        f"Train loss: {train_loss_sum / train_count:.4f} | "
        f"Train accuracy: {train_correct / train_count:.2%} | "
        f"Val loss: {val_loss_sum / val_count:.4f} | "
        f"Val accuracy: {val_correct / val_count:.2%}"
    )

    train_with_reg_accuracy_history.append(train_correct / train_count)
    val_with_reg_accuracy_history.append(val_correct / val_count)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)

num_epochs = 25
best_parameters = model.parameters()
patience = 3
previous_val_loss = float("inf")
no_improvement = 0
change_threshold = 0.05

train_with_early_stop_loss_history = []
val_with_early_stop_loss_history = []

train_with_stop_accuracy_history = []
val_with_stop_accuracy_history = []

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    train_loss_sum = 0.0
    train_correct = 0
    train_count = 0

    for inputs, targets in train_loader:
        inputs = inputs.to(device)
        targets = targets.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        batch_size = targets.size(0)
        train_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
        train_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
        train_count += batch_size

    best_parameters = model.parameters()

    model.eval()
    val_loss_sum = 0.0
    val_correct = 0

            batch_size = targets.size(0)
            val_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
            val_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
            val_count += batch_size

    # Check if the current average validation loss is less than the previous loss
    if abs((val_loss_sum / val_count) - previous_val_loss) < change_threshold:
        no_improvement += 1
    else:
        best_parameters = model.parameters()
    previous_val_loss = val_loss_sum / val_count

    # Break the loop if this is the third time the validation loss hasn't changed
    if no_improvement == patience:
        break

    train_with_early_stop_loss_history.append(train_loss_sum / train_count)
    val_with_early_stop_loss_history.append(val_loss_sum / val_count)

        f"Val accuracy: {val_correct / val_count:.2%} | "

    )

# Reuse the existing stratified split.
X_train = train_ds["img"]

coarse_train = train_ds["coarse_label"]

X_valid = valid_ds["img"]
fine_valid = valid_ds["fine_label"]
coarse_valid = valid_ds["coarse_label"]

class FineCoarseDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y, z):
        self.features = X
        self.fine_labels = y
        self.coarse_labels = z
        self.transform = transforms.Compose([
            transforms.ToTensor(),
            transforms.Normalize(
                (0.5071, 0.4867, 0.4408),
                (0.2675, 0.2565, 0.2761)
            ),
        ])

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        image = self.features[index]

        # Handles PIL images or original uint8 image arrays.
        if not isinstance(image, Image.Image):
            image = Image.fromarray(np.asarray(image))

        image = self.transform(image.convert("RGB"))
        fine_label = torch.tensor(int(self.fine_labels[index]), dtype=torch.long)
        coarse_label = torch.tensor(int(self.coarse_labels[index]), dtype=torch.long)
        return image, fine_label, coarse_label

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.features)


train_dataset = FineCoarseDataset(X_train, fine_train, coarse_train)
val_dataset = FineCoarseDataset(X_valid, fine_valid, coarse_valid)

train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True
)
val_loader = DataLoader(
    val_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=False
)

class dual_output_model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(512, 256),
            nn.ReLU(),
        )
        
        self.fine_layer = nn.Linear(256, 100)
        self.coarse_layer = nn.Linear(256, 20)

    def forward(self, x):
        hidden_results = self.hidden_layers(x)

        fine_results = self.fine_layer(hidden_results)
        coarse_results = self.coarse_layer(hidden_results)

        return fine_results, coarse_results


model = dual_output_model().to(device)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

num_epochs = 25

val_with_multi_task_loss_history = []

        fine_loss = criterion(fine_outputs, fine_targets)
        coarse_loss = criterion(coarse_outputs, coarse_targets)
        loss = fine_loss + coarse_loss
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        batch_size = fine_targets.size(0)
        train_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
        train_correct += (fine_outputs.argmax(dim=1) == fine_targets).sum().item()
        train_count += batch_size

    model.eval()
    val_loss_sum = 0.0
    val_correct = 0
    val_count = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, fine_targets, coarse_targets in val_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            fine_targets = fine_targets.to(device)
            coarse_targets = coarse_targets.to(device)

            fine_outputs, coarse_outputs = model(inputs)
            
            fine_loss = criterion(fine_outputs, fine_targets)

    train_with_multi_task_loss_history.append(train_loss_sum / train_count)

title: Fall 2026 CSC-372 Project Part 7
text:
7. Transfer learning
Use a ResNet-18 pretrained on ImageNet. Freeze its existing layers and replace its final classification layer with a new layer that predicts the 100 CIFAR-100 classes. Train only this new layer.
Compare its training–test loss and accuracy gaps with the baseline.
Because this experiment changes both the architecture and the initial weights, differences from the baseline cannot be attributed to pretraining alone.
Does the pretrained model reduce the generalization gap? Does it also change training and test performance?

Step 1: Load the pretrained model
The pretrained model has already learned image features from ImageNet. We will reuse those features and train a new final classifier for CIFAR-100.

import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from torchvision.models import resnet18, ResNet18_Weights

weights = ResNet18_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1
transfer_model = resnet18(weights=weights)

print(transfer_model.fc)



model = transfer_model
model.eval()

image = ds["test"][0]["img"].convert("RGB")  # One CIFAR-100 image
x = weights.transforms()(image)             # Resize, crop, normalize
x = x.unsqueeze(0)                          # Add batch dimension

with torch.no_grad():
    scores = model(x)

predicted_class = scores.argmax(dim=1).item()

print("Input shape:", x.shape)       # [1, 3, 224, 224]
print("Output shape:", scores.shape) # [1, 1000]
print("Prediction:", weights.meta["categories"][predicted_class])

The original final layer predicts 1,000 ImageNet classes. We need 100 outputs instead.


Step 2: Freeze the existing layers and replace the classifier**
requires_grad = False prevents the optimizer from updating the pretrained parameters. The new layer has trainable parameters by default.

# Freeze all existing parameters.
for parameter in transfer_model.parameters():
    parameter.requires_grad = False

# Replace the original classifier with a trainable CIFAR-100 classifier.
num_features = transfer_model.fc.in_features
transfer_model.fc = nn.Linear(num_features, 100)

transfer_model = transfer_model.to(device)

print("New classifier:", transfer_model.fc)
print(
    "Trainable parameters:",
    sum(p.numel() for p in transfer_model.parameters()
        if p.requires_grad)
)

The order matters: freeze the existing model before creating the new layer.


Step 3: Prepare images for the pretrained model
Use the preprocessing supplied with the pretrained weights. It resizes and center-crops images to 224 × 224, converts them into tensors, and applies ImageNet normalization. Use the same preprocessing for training, validation, and testing in this experiment.

transfer_transform = weights.transforms()


class TransferDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, rows):
        self.rows = rows

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.rows)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        example = self.rows[int(index)]

        image = example["img"].convert("RGB")
        image = transfer_transform(image)

        label = int(example["fine_label"])
        return image, label


# Reuse the existing stratified split. Do not split the data again.
transfer_train_dataset = TransferDataset(train_ds)
transfer_valid_dataset = TransferDataset(valid_ds)
transfer_test_dataset = TransferDataset(test_ds)

transfer_train_loader = DataLoader(
    transfer_train_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True
)

transfer_valid_loader = DataLoader(
    transfer_valid_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=False
)

transfer_test_loader = DataLoader(
    transfer_test_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=False
)

If memory is limited, reduce the batch size and document the change.


Step 4: Define the loss, optimizer, and evaluation function
The model returns raw class scores, so use cross-entropy directly. Only the new classifier is passed to the optimizer.

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(
    transfer_model.fc.parameters(),
    lr=1e-3
)

criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()


def evaluate_transfer(model, loader):
    model.eval()

    loss_sum = 0.0
    correct = 0
    count = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for images, labels in loader:
            images = images.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            logits = model(images)
            loss = criterion(logits, labels)

            count += labels.size(0)
            loss_sum += loss.item() * labels.size(0)
            correct += (logits.argmax(dim=1) == labels).sum().item()

    return loss_sum / count, correct / count



Step 5: Train the new classifier
Keep the frozen model in evaluation mode while training the classifier. ResNet contains batch-normalization layers whose stored statistics would otherwise change during training.
eval() does not disable gradients: the new classifier can still learn

Output shape: torch.Size([1, 1000])
Prediction: volcano

text:
10. Noise on weights
Train the baseline model with temporary Gaussian noise added to its weights before each forward pass:
\[
\tilde{w} = w + 0.05\,|w|\,z,
\qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).
\]
Sample fresh noise for each training batch. After loss.backward(), restore the original weights before calling optimizer.step().
Evaluate using clean weights. Compare the training–test loss and accuracy gaps with the baseline.
Add noise using torch.randn_like(x). Randn_like generates a tensor of the same shape as x with elements drawn from a standard normal distribution i.e. with mean 0 and variance 1.
For example, for a weight tensor w, you can add noise as
z = torch.randn_like(w)
w_noisy = w + 0.05 * w.abs() * z
Does weight noise reduce the generalization gap?

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(32 * 32 * 3, 512),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(512, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 100),
).to(device)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

num_epochs = 25

train_with_noisy_weight_loss_history = []
val_with_noisy_weight_loss_history = []

train_with_noisy_weight_accuracy_history = []
val_with_noisy_weight_accuracy_history = []

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    train_loss_sum = 0.0
    train_correct = 0
    train_count = 0

    for inputs, targets in train_loader:
        inputs = inputs.to(device)
        targets = targets.to(device)

        noise_values = []
        with torch.no_grad():
            for w in model.parameters():
                # Sample the noise to add
                z = torch.rand_like(w)
                # Calculate the change
                change = 0.5 * w.abs() * w
                # Add the change of the weight in-place
                w.add_(change)
                noise_values.append(change)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
        loss.backward()

        with torch.no_grad():
            for w, change in zip(model.parameters(), noise_values):
                # Remove the noise from the weight
                w.sub_(change)

        optimizer.step()

        batch_size = targets.size(0)
        train_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
        train_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
        train_count += batch_size

    model.eval()
    val_loss_sum = 0.0
    val_correct = 0
    val_count = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, targets in val_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            targets = targets.to(device)

            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

            batch_size = targets.size(0)
            val_loss_sum += loss.item() * batch_size
            val_correct += (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == targets).sum().item()
            val_count += batch_size

    train_with_noisy_weight_loss_history.append(train_loss_sum / train_count)
    val_with_noisy_weight_loss_history.append(val_loss_sum / val_count)

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch + 1}/{num_epochs} | "
        f"Train loss: {train_loss_sum / train_count:.4f} | "
        f"Train accuracy: {train_correct / train_count:.2%} | "
        f"Val loss: {val_loss_sum / val_count:.4f} | "
        f"Val accuracy: {val_correct / val_count:.2%}"
    )

    train_with_noisy_weight_accuracy_history.append(train_correct / train_count)
    val_with_noisy_weight_accuracy_history.append(val_correct / val_count)

title: Attention
text:
To motivate the need for attention mechanisms, consider the following passage:

The restaurant refused to serve me a ham sandwich because it only serves vegetarian food. In the end, they just gave me two slices of bread. Their ambiance was just as good as the food and service.

The goal is to design a network to process this text into a representation suitable for downstream tasks.
For example, it might be used to classify the review as positive or negative or to answer questions such as “Does the restaurant serve steak?”.



We can make three immediate observations:

First, the encoded input can be surprisingly large. In this case, each of the 37 words might be represented by an embedding vector of length 1024, so the encoded input would be of length 37×1024 = 37888 even for this small passage.
A more realistically sized body of text might have hundreds or even thousands of words, so fully connected neural networks are impractical.
Second, one of the defining characteristics of NLP problems is that each input (one or more sentences) is of a different length.
It is not even obvious how to apply a fully connected network.
These observations suggest that the network should share parameters across words at different input positions.
Third, language is ambiguous; it is unclear that the pronoun it refers to the restaurant and not to the ham sandwich. To understand the text, the word it should somehow be connected to the word restaurant.
In the parlance of transformers, the former word should pay attention to the latter. This implies that there must be connections between the words and that the strength of these connections will depend on the words themselves. Moreover, these connections need to extend across large text spans. For example, the word their in the last sentence also refers to the restaurant.









Linguistic phenomenon
Example
Connection to learn




Pronoun resolution
The dog chased the cat because it was frightened.
What does it refer to?


Pronoun resolution
Sarah called Emma after she finished work.
Which person finished work?


Subject–verb agreement
The keys to the old cabinet are missing.
Are must agree with keys, not cabinet.


Adjective modification
The old man carried a heavy suitcase.
Which noun does each adjective describe?


Adverb modification
She barely passed the exam.
Barely changes how we interpret passed.


Negation
The movie was not particularly interesting.
Not reverses the evaluation.


Word-sense disambiguation
He sat by the bank and watched the river.
River helps determine the meaning of bank.


Word-sense disambiguation
She deposited money at the bank.
Money and deposited indicate a financial institution.


Long-distance dependency
The book that the professor recommended yesterday was fascinating.
Was relates to book, despite intervening words.


Semantic roles
The chef cooked the fish with a pan.
Pan is an instrument used for cooking.


Semantic roles
The chef cooked the fish with lemon.
Lemon is an ingredient or accompaniment.


Contrast
Although the restaurant was expensive, the food was excellent.
Although signals a contrast between clauses.


Coreference across sentences
John bought a bicycle. He rode it home.
He connects to John; it to bicycle.


Conditional relationships
If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
If establishes a dependency between clauses.



The central teaching point is that a token’s representation should depend not only on the token itself, but also on other relevant tokens in the sequence.
