title: Masked Attention
text:
Masked attention is used to prevent attending to certain positions, typically future positions in sequence modeling tasks. This is commonly used in autoregressive models where the prediction for a position should not depend on future positions. A mask is applied to the attention scores before the softmax operation, setting the scores of the masked positions to a very large negative value, effectively ignoring them during attention computation.

Interaction matrices for self-attention. a) In an encoder, every token interacts with every other token, and computation expands quadratically with the number of tokens. b) In a decoder, each token only interacts with the previous tokens, but complexity is still quadratic. c) Complexity can be reduced by using a convolutional structure (encoder case). d) Convolutional structure for decoder case. e–f) Convolutional structure with dilation rate of two and three (decoder case). g) Another strategy is to allow selected tokens to interact with all the other tokens (encoder case) or all the previous tokens (decoder case pictured). h) Alternatively, global tokens can be introduced (left two columns and top two rows). These interact with all of the tokens as well as with each other.

title: Transformers
text:
Types of Transformers
Finally, the embedding matrix X representing the text is passed through a series of K transformer layers, called a transformer model. There are three types of transformer models:

Encoder: An encoder transforms the text embeddings into a representation that can support a variety of tasks.
Decoder: A decoder predicts the next token to continue the input text.
Encoder-decoder: Encoder-decoders are used in sequence-to-sequence tasks, where one text string is converted into another (e.g., machine translation).









Architecture
Attention pattern
Example task




Encoder-only
Usually bidirectional self-attention
Classification or masked-token prediction


Decoder-only
Causal self-attention
Text generation


Encoder–decoder
Encoder self-attention, causal decoder self-attention, and cross-attention
Translation

title: Transformers
text:
Layer Normalization (LayerNorm)
Suppose a token has a four-dimensional embedding:
\[ x=[2,4,6,8] \]
Its mean is:
\[ \mu=\frac{2+4+6+8}{4}=5 \]
Its standard deviation is:
\[ \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{(2-5)^2+(4-5)^2+(6-5)^2+(8-5)^2}{4}}=\sqrt{5} \]
LayerNorm first standardizes the vector:
\[ \hat{x}=\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}} \]
Ignoring the tiny \(\) for simplicity:
\[ \hat{x}\approx[-1.34,-0.45,0.45,1.34] \]
Now the vector has approximately:

Mean = 0
Standard deviation = 1

But LayerNorm doesn’t stop there. It also learns a scale and shift for each dimension:
\[ \boxed{y=\gamma\odot\hat{x}+\beta} \]
Here, \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learnable parameters, each with four elements in this example. They allow the network to adjust the standardized representation.
What exactly gets normalized in a transformer?
Suppose the input has shape:
\[ (\text{batch},\text{tokens},\text{embedding dimensions}) =(32,64,128) \]
LayerNorm normalizes each token’s 128-dimensional vector independently.
LayerNorm operates across embedding dimensions
Each row is normalized separately. The same learned γ and β parameters are shared across token positions.
This is different from Batch Normalization, which uses statistics across examples in a batch.
Where does LayerNorm appear in our transformer?
Recall our implementation:
attention_output = self.attention(x)
x = self.norm1(x + attention_output)
ff_output = self.feedforward(x)
x = self.norm2(x + ff_output)
The first LayerNorm normalizes the result of the attention block plus its residual connection.
The second normalizes the result of the feed-forward block plus its residual connection.
This is called a Post-LayerNorm transformer, because normalization happens after each residual addition. Many modern transformer architectures instead use Pre-LayerNorm, which normalizes before each sublayer.
PyTorch implementation
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
x = torch.tensor([[2., 4., 6., 8.]])
norm = nn.LayerNorm(4)
y = norm(x)
print(y)
The important detail is that nn.LayerNorm(4) creates 8 learnable parameters:

Four scale parameters (\(\))
Four shift parameters (\(\))

For our transformer with d_model=128, each LayerNorm has 256 learnable parameters.
Why do we need it?
During training, the outputs of attention and feed-forward layers can change in magnitude as their parameters are updated. LayerNorm helps keep the scale of representations more controlled, making optimization more stable.
It also helps gradients propagate through deep transformer networks.
One important distinction: LayerNorm does not make all token embeddings identical or erase their contextual information. It normalizes each vector’s mean and variance, while preserving differences in the relative values of its dimensions.
In short, self-attention determines what information each token receives; LayerNorm helps keep the resulting representations numerically well-behaved.

title: Transformers
text:
Residual connections
Residual connections are a key component of transformer layers. They allow the network to retain information from earlier layers by adding the input of a layer to its output. This helps mitigate the vanishing gradient problem and enables the training of very deep networks.
Mathematically, if a layer implements a function \(F(\mathbf{X})\), the residual connection produces an output \(\mathbf{X} + F(\mathbf{X})\). In transformers, both the multi-head self-attention and the feed-forward sub-layers use residual connections.

title: Transformers
text:
Transformer layers
Self-attention is just one part of a larger transformer layer. This consists of a multi- head self-attention unit (which allows the word representations to interact with each other) followed by a fully connected network \(\textbf{mlp}[\mathbf{x}_\bullet]\) (that operates separately on each word). Both units are residual networks (i.e., their output is added back to the original input). In addition, it is typical to add a LayerNorm operation after both the self- attention and fully connected networks. This is similar to BatchNorm but normalizes each embedding in each batch element separately using statistics calculated across its D embedding dimensions (section 11.4 and figure 11.14). The complete layer can be described by the following series of operations (figure 12.7):

Transformer layer. The input consists of a D × N matrix containing the D-dimensional word embeddings for each of the N input tokens. The output is a matrix of the same size. The transformer layer consists of a series of operations. First, there is a multi-head attention block, allowing the word embeddings to interact with one another. This forms the processing of a residual block, so the inputs are added back to the output. Second, a LayerNorm operation is applied separately to each embedding. Third, there is a second residual layer where the same fully connected neural network is applied separately to each of the N word representations (columns). Finally, LayerNorm is applied again.
\[\begin{eqnarray}
  \mathbf{X} &\leftarrow& \mathbf{X} + \mbox{\bf{MhSa}}[\mathbf{X}] \nonumber \\
  \mathbf{X} &\leftarrow& \mbox{\bf{LayerNorm}}[\mathbf{X}] \hspace{3cm}\nonumber\\
  \mathbf{x}_{n} &\leftarrow& \mathbf{x}_{n}+\mbox{\bf{mlp}}[\mathbf{x}_{n}] \hspace{3.6cm}\forall\; n\in\{1,\ldots, N\}\nonumber\\
  \mathbf{X} &\leftarrow& \mbox{\bf{LayerNorm}}[\mathbf{X}],
\end{eqnarray}\]
where the column vectors xn are separately taken from the full data matrix X. In a real network, the data passes through a series of these transformer layers.

title: Multi-Head Attention
text:
Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. Instead of performing a single attention function, the queries, keys, and values are projected into multiple subspaces, and attention is applied in parallel across these subspaces. The outputs are then concatenated and linearly transformed.
Multiple self-attention mechanisms are usually applied in parallel, and this is known as multi-head self-attention. Now \(H\) different sets of values, keys, and queries are computed:
\[\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbf{V}_h &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{vh}\mathbf{1}^{T}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{\mathit{vh}}\mathbf{X}\nonumber \\
\mathbf{Q}_h &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{qh}\mathbf{1}^{T}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{\mathit{qh}}\mathbf{X}\nonumber \\
\mathbf{K}_h &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{kh}\mathbf{1}^{T}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{\mathit{kh}}\mathbf{X}.
\end{eqnarray}\]
The \(h\)th self-attention mechanism or head can be written as:
\[\begin{eqnarray}
  \mbox{{\bf Sa}}_{h}[\mathbf{X}] =\mathbf{V}_h\cdot\mbox{\bf Softmax}\left[\frac{\mathbf{K}_h^{T}\mathbf{Q}_h}{\sqrt{D}_{q}}\right],
\end{eqnarray}\]
where we have different parameters \(\{\boldsymbol\beta_{vh},\boldsymbol\Omega_{vh}\}\), \(\{\boldsymbol\beta_{qh},\boldsymbol\Omega_{qh}\}\), and \(\{\boldsymbol\beta_{kh},\boldsymbol\Omega_{kh}\}\) for each head. Typically, if the dimension of the inputs \(\mathbf{x}_m\) is \(D\) and there are \(H\) heads, the values, queries, and keys will all be of size \(D/H\), as this allows for an eﬀicient implementation. The outputs of these self-attention mechanisms are vertically concatenated, and another linear transform \(\boldsymbol\Omega_c\) is applied to combine them (figure 12.6):

Multi-head self-attention. Self-attention occurs in parallel across multiple “heads.” Each has its own queries, keys, and values. Here two heads are depicted, in the cyan and orange boxes, respectively. The outputs are vertically concatenated, and another linear transformation Ωc is used to recombine them.
\[\begin{eqnarray}
  \mbox{{\bf MhSa}}[\mathbf{X}] = \boldsymbol\Omega_{c}\Bigl[\mbox{{\bf Sa}}_{1}[\mathbf{X}]^T,\mbox{{\bf Sa}}_{2}[\mathbf{X}]^T,\ldots,\mbox{{\bf Sa}}_{H}[\mathbf{X}]^T \Bigr]^T.
\end{eqnarray}\]
Multiple heads seem to be necessary to make self-attention work well. It has been speculated that they make the self-attention network more robust to bad initializations.
Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) is a technique used in neural networks to keep the values of a vector on a consistent scale. It is particularly important in transformers because it helps stabilize training.
The intuition is simple: take a vector, subtract its mean, and divide by its standard deviation.
The multihead self-attention mechanism maps \(N\) inputs \(\mathbf{x_n} \in \mathbb{R}^D\) and returns N outputs \(\mathbf{x^{\prime}} \in \mathbb{R}^D\) .


import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Set seed so we get the same random numbers
np.random.seed(3)
# Number of inputs
N = 6
# Number of dimensions of each input
D = 8
# Create an empty list
X = np.random.normal(size=(D,N))
# Print X
print(X)

We’ll use two heads. We’ll need the weights and biases for the keys, queries, and values (equations 12.2 and 12.4). We’ll use two heads, and (as in the figure), we’ll make the queries keys and values of size D/H

# Number of heads
H = 2
# QDV dimension
H_D = int(D/H)

# Set seed so we get the same random numbers
np.random.seed(0)

# Choose random values for the parameters for the first head
omega_q1 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,D))
omega_k1 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,D))
omega_v1 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,D))
beta_q1 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,1))
beta_k1 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,1))
beta_v1 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,1))

# Choose random values for the parameters for the second head
omega_q2 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,D))
omega_k2 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,D))
omega_v2 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,D))
beta_q2 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,1))
beta_k2 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,1))
beta_v2 = np.random.normal(size=(H_D,1))

# Choose random values for the parameters
omega_c = np.random.normal(size=(D,D))

Now let’s compute the multiscale self-attention

# Define softmax operation that works independently on each column
def softmax_cols(data_in):
  # Exponentiate all of the values
  exp_values = np.exp(data_in) ;
  # Sum over columns
  denom = np.sum(exp_values, axis = 0);
  # Compute softmax (numpy broadcasts denominator to all rows automatically)
  softmax = exp_values / denom
  # return the answer
  return softmax


# Now let's compute multihead scaled self-attention in matrix form
def multihead_scaled_self_attention(X, omega_v1, omega_q1, omega_k1, beta_v1, beta_q1, beta_k1,
                                       omega_v2, omega_q2, omega_k2, beta_v2, beta_q2, beta_k2, omega_c):

  # Head 1: queries, keys, values (each H_D x N)
  Q1 = omega_q1 @ X + beta_q1
  K1 = omega_k1 @ X + beta_k1
  V1 = omega_v1 @ X + beta_v1
  # Scaled dot products (N x N): row m = key m, column n = query n
  # softmax_cols normalizes each column, i.e. over keys for each query
  head1 = V1 @ softmax_cols(K1.T @ Q1 / np.sqrt(Q1.shape[0]))

  # Head 2
  Q2 = omega_q2 @ X + beta_q2
  K2 = omega_k2 @ X + beta_k2
  V2 = omega_v2 @ X + beta_v2
  head2 = V2 @ softmax_cols(K2.T @ Q2 / np.sqrt(Q2.shape[0]))

  # Vertically concatenate heads (D x N) and recombine
  X_prime = omega_c @ np.vstack([head1, head2])

  return X_prime

# Run the self attention mechanism
X_prime = multihead_scaled_self_attention(X,omega_v1, omega_q1, omega_k1, beta_v1, beta_q1, beta_k1, omega_v2, omega_q2, omega_k2, beta_v2, beta_q2, beta_k2, omega_c)

# Print out the results
np.set_printoptions(precision=3)
print("Your answer:")
print(X_prime)

title: Cross-Attention
text: Cross-attention. The flow of computation is the same as in standard self-attention, but the queries are calculated from the decoder embeddings Xdec, and the keys and values from the encoder embeddings Xenc. For translation tasks, the encoder contains information about the source language statistics, and the decoder contains information about the target language statistics.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
text:
Dot product attention computes the similarity between queries and keys using the dot product. The attention weights are then obtained by applying the softmax function to these dot products.






Dot Product Primer





In machine learning, data points are often represented as vectors in a high-dimensional space. For example, word embeddings represent words as vectors, with semantically related words often occupying nearby regions of the embedding space. To compare two vectors, we need a way to measure how similar they are.
Three commonly used measures are Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, and dot product. Although closely related mathematically, they capture different aspects of the relationship between vectors.


Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between two points in space.
For two vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\):
\[
d(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d}(a_i-b_i)^2}
\]
A smaller distance indicates that the vectors are closer together. Euclidean distance considers both the direction and magnitude of the vectors.



Cosine similarity measures the angle between two nonzero vectors, regardless of their magnitudes.
\[
\cos(\theta)=\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|}
\]

1: Vectors point in the same direction.
0: Vectors are perpendicular.
−1: Vectors point in opposite directions.

For example, the vectors \([1,2]\) and \([10,20]\) have a cosine similarity of 1, even though they are far apart in Euclidean distance.
Cosine similarity is particularly useful when the direction of a vector is more important than its magnitude.



The dot product of two vectors is calculated by multiplying corresponding components and summing the results:
\[
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_i b_i
\]
Geometrically, the dot product can also be expressed as:
\[
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos(\theta)
\]
This reveals an important relationship: the dot product combines angular alignment (cosine similarity) with vector magnitudes.
Two vectors have a large positive dot product when they point in similar directions and have large magnitudes. Their dot product is zero when they are perpendicular and negative when they point in opposing directions.
Unlike cosine similarity, the dot product is not normalized. Consequently, two vectors can have a high dot product because of their magnitudes, even if they are not especially well aligned.



Consider three vectors:
\[
\mathbf{a}=[1,2],\quad \mathbf{b}=[2,4],\quad \mathbf{c}=[-2,1]
\]



Comparison
Euclidean Distance
Cosine Similarity
Dot Product




a vs. b
2.24
1.0
10


a vs. c
3.16
0.0
0



Vectors a and b point in exactly the same direction, giving them a cosine similarity of 1, but they have different magnitudes and therefore a nonzero Euclidean distance. Vectors a and c are perpendicular, so both their cosine similarity and dot product are zero.
Key takeaway: Euclidean distance measures proximity, cosine similarity measures directional alignment, and dot product measures alignment weighted by magnitude. For unit-length vectors, dot product and cosine similarity are identical.




Dot Product is preferred when the dimensionality of the queries and keys is not too large, as it is computationally efficient and works well in practice.


Other measures of similarity between queries and keys include additive attention, cosine similarity, and learned compatibility functions.
These mechanisms can be used when dot product attention is not suitable or when different properties are desired.
Additive attention computes the similarity between queries and keys using a feed-forward neural network. It is often used when the dimensionality of the queries and keys is large, as it can be more stable than dot product attention.
\[
\text{Additive Attention: } \text{score}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) = \mathbf{v}^\top \tanh(\mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{k})
\]
Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between queries and keys, effectively normalizing their magnitudes. It is useful when the direction of the vectors is more important than their magnitude.
\[
\text{Cosine Similarity: } \text{score}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}}{\|\mathbf{q}\| \|\mathbf{k}\|}
\]
Learned compatibility functions use a parameterized function to compute the similarity between queries and keys. This allows the model to learn the most appropriate similarity measure for the task at hand.
\[
\text{Learned Compatibility: } \text{score}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) = f_\theta(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k})
\]

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
text:
Scaled Attention
The passage compresses three ideas: why the dot products get large, why large inputs make softmax “saturate,” and why saturation kills gradients. Taking them in order:

1. Dot products grow with dimension
Suppose each component of a query \(\mathbf{q}\) and a key \(\mathbf{k}\) is roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1. That’s approximately true at initialization with standard weight init and normalized inputs. Their dot product is
\[\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k} = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i\]
Each term \(q_i k_i\) has mean 0 and variance 1, and you’re summing \(d_k\) of them. So the dot product has variance \(d_k\), or standard deviation \(\sqrt{d_k}\).
With \(d_k = 64\), typical attention logits are around ±8. With \(d_k = 512\), they’re around ±23. Nothing has been learned yet; the size comes purely from the dimension.


2. Large logits make softmax nearly one-hot
Softmax depends on the differences between its inputs, and it’s exponential in them. Compare one query’s logits against three keys:



logits
softmax output




[8, 0, −8] (unscaled, \(d_k=64\))
[0.9997, 0.0003, 0.0000001]


[1, 0, −1] (divided by \(\sqrt{64}=8\))
[0.665, 0.245, 0.090]



In the unscaled case, the query attends to one key and ignores everything else. The model never made that decision; it’s an artifact of the logit scale.
3. A one-hot softmax has near-zero gradients
This is the key step. Training works by asking: if I nudge this input a little, how much does the output change? That sensitivity is the gradient. If the answer is “barely at all,” the model gets almost no signal about which direction to adjust.
A nudge experiment. Take the logits from the example above and increase the second one by 1:










before nudge
after nudge
change in 2nd weight




Unscaled
[8, 0, −8] → weights [0.9997, 0.0003, 0.0000]
[8, 1, −8] → weights [0.9991, 0.0009, 0.0000]
+0.0006


Scaled
[1, 0, −1] → weights [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]
[1, 1, −1] → weights [0.468, 0.468, 0.063]
+0.22



The same nudge moves the scaled attention weight about 370 times more. When one logit dominates, softmax is “stuck”: the winner already has nearly all the weight and the others have nearly none, so small changes in either direction hardly register.
4. Why \(\sqrt{d_k}\) specifically
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) divides by the standard deviation of the dot product, which brings the variance back to 1 regardless of dimension:
\[\text{Var}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \frac{d_k}{d_k} = 1\]
Dividing by \(d_k\) would overshoot: the variance becomes \(1/d_k\), the logits all sit near zero, and attention becomes nearly uniform. Not scaling at all leaves softmax saturated. The \(\sqrt{d_k}\) factor is exactly what keeps logits in the range where softmax is sensitive.

title: Self-Attention
text:
The previous section argued that a model for processing text will

use parameter sharing to cope with long input passages of differing lengths and
contain connections between word representations that depend on the words themselves.

The transformer acquires both properties by using dot-product self-attention.


Value Vectors
Value vectors in the context of self-attention are adjusted embeddings of the input tokens, capturing their information or semantics in a form that can be effectively combined with other tokens’ information (through the attention mechanism). In other words, the value vector still satisfy the property that similar input tokens have similar value vectors.
First, a set of Value vectors are computed for each input:
\[\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq:transformer_values}
  \mathbf{v}_{m} = \boldsymbol\beta_{v}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{v}\mathbf{x}_{m},
\end{eqnarray}\]
where \(\boldsymbol\beta_{v} ∈ \mathbb{R}^{D×1}\) and \(\boldsymbol\Omega_{v} ∈ \mathbb{R}^{D×D}\) represent biases and weights, respectively.
Note that the subscript \(m\) in \(\mathbf{v}_{m}\) corresponds to the mth input \(\mathbf{x}_{m}\) and \(m \in \{1, \ldots, N\}\). More importantly note that only the value vector \(\mathbf{v}_{m}\) and input vector \(\mathbf{x}_{m}\) have the subscript \(m\). Both beta and Omega do not have the subscript \(m\) but have the subscripts \(v\) to indicate that they are associated with the value vectors and not specific to any particular input. In other words, the same parameters \(\boldsymbol\beta_{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol\Omega_{v}\) are shared by all inputs.



Contrast this with a fully connected layer. In case of a fully connected layer, the weight matrix \(\Omega\) would have been dense and of dimension \((N\times D) \times (N\times D)\). In self-attention, however, the weights \(\boldsymbol\Omega_{v}\) are shared across all inputs, which allows the model to maintain permutation invariance and efficiently handle variable-length sequences.
Therefore, the equation \(\mathbf{v}_{m} = \boldsymbol\beta_{v}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{v}\mathbf{x}_{m}\) shows that the same weights \(\Omega_v ∈ \mathbb{R}^{D×D}\) and biases \(\beta_v ∈ \mathbb{R}^{D}\) are applied to each input \(x_• \in \mathbb{R}^{D}\).
This computation scales linearly with the sequence length N, so it needs fewer parameters than a fully connected network relating all DN inputs to all DN values.
In fact, the value computation can be viewed as a sparse matrix operation with shared parameters that relates these DN quantities (figure 12.2b).


Self-Attention Block
A self-attention block \(\mathbf{sa}[•]\) takes N inputs \(\mathbf{x}_1,...,\mathbf{x}_N\), each of dimension \(D\times 1\),and returns N outputs \(\mathbf{sa}_1[\mathbf{x}_1,...,\mathbf{x}_N],...,\mathbf{sa}_N[\mathbf{x}_1,...,\mathbf{x}_N]\), each of which is also of size \(D\times 1\). 
\(D\) is the embedding dimension of each token and \(N\) is the number of input tokens.
Then the nth output \(\mathbf{sa}_{n}[\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots, \mathbf{x}_{N}]\) is a weighted sum of all the values \(\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{N}\):
\[\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq:transformer_sattention1}
  \mbox{{\bf sa}}_{n}[\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots, \mathbf{x}_{N}] = \sum_{m=1}^{N}a[\mathbf{x}_{m}, \mathbf{x}_{n}]\mathbf{v}_{m}.
\end{eqnarray}\]
The scalar weight a[\(\mathbf{x}_{m},\mathbf{x}_{n}\)] is the attention that the nth output pays to input \(\mathbf{x}_{m}\).
The \(N\) weights \(a[•,\mathbf{x}_{n}]\) are non-negative and sum to one.
Hence, self-attention can be thought of as routing the values in different proportions to create each output (figure 12.1).
The attention weights \(a[\mathbf{x}_m,\mathbf{x}_n]\) combine the values from different inputs.
They are also sparse since there is only one weight for each ordered pair of inputs \((\mathbf{x}_m,\mathbf{x}_n)\), regardless of the size of these inputs (figure 12.2c).
It follows that the number of attention weights has a quadratic dependence on the sequence length N, but is independent of the length D of each input.


Self-attention as routing. The self-attention mechanism takes N inputs \(\mathbf{x}_1, . . . , \mathbf{x}_N ∈ \mathbb{R}^{D}\) (here N = 3 and D = 4) and processes each separately to compute N value vectors.
The nth output \(\mathbf{sa}_{n}[\mathbf{x}_1, . . . , \mathbf{x}_N]\) (written as \(\mathbf{sa}_{n}[\mathbf{x}_•]\) for short) is then computed as a weighted sum of the N value vectors, where the weights are positive and sum to one.

Output \(\mathbf{sa}_{1}[\mathbf{x}_•]\) is computed as \(a[\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_1] =
0.1\) times the first value vector, \(a[\mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_1] = 0.3\) times the second value vector, and \(a[\mathbf{x}_3, \mathbf{x}_1] = 0.6\) times the third value vector.
Output \(\mathbf{sa}_{2}[\mathbf{x}_•]\) is computed in the same way, but this time with weights of \(0.5, 0.2\), and \(0.3\).
The weighting for output \(\mathbf{sa}_{3}[\mathbf{x}_•]\) is different again. Each output can hence be thought of as a different routing of the N values.



Self-attention for N =3 inputs \(\mathbf{x}_n\), each with dimension D=4.

Each input \(\mathbf{x}_m\) is operated on independently by the same weights \(\Omega_v\) (same color equals same weight) and biases \(\beta_v\) (not shown) to form the values \(\beta_v + \Omega_v\mathbf{x}_m\).
Each output is a linear combination of the values, with the attention weight \(a[\mathbf{x}_m, \mathbf{x}_n]\) defining the contribution of the \(m\)th value to the \(n\)th output.
Matrix showing block sparsity of linear transformation \(\Omega_v\) between inputs and values.
Matrix showing sparsity of attention weights relating values and outputs.




Query vectors, Key vectors and Attention Weights
In the previous section, we saw that the outputs result from two chained linear transformations; the value vectors \(\beta_v + \Omega_v \mathbf{x}_m\) are computed independently for each input \(\mathbf{x}_m\), and these vectors are combined linearly by the attention weights \(a[\mathbf{x}_m,\mathbf{x}_n]\).

To compute the attention, we apply two more linear transformations to the inputs:
\[\begin{eqnarray}
  \mathbf{q}_{n} &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{q}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{q}\mathbf{x}_{n}\nonumber \\
  \mathbf{k}_{m} &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{k}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{k}\mathbf{x}_{m},
\end{eqnarray}\]
where \(\mathbf{q}_n\) and \(\mathbf{k}_m\) are termed queries and keys, respectively. Then we compute dot products between the queries and keys and pass the results through a softmax function:
\[\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq:transformer_sattention2}
  a[\mathbf{x}_{m},\mathbf{x}_{n}] &=& \mbox{softmax}_{m}\left[\mathbf{k}_{\bullet}^{T}\mathbf{q}_{n}\right]\nonumber\\
  \\
  &=& \frac{\exp\left[\mathbf{k}_{m}^{T}\mathbf{q}_{n}\right]}{\sum_{m'=1}^{N}\exp\left[\mathbf{k}_{m'}^{T}\mathbf{q}_{n} \right]},
\end{eqnarray}\]
so for each \(\mathbf{x}_n\), they are positive and sum to one (figure 12.3). For obvious reasons, this is known as dot-product self-attention.
The names “queries” and “keys” were inherited from the field of information retrieval and have the following interpretation: the dot product operation returns a measure of similarity between its inputs, so the weights \(a[\mathbf{x}_\bullet,\mathbf{x}_n]\) depend on the relative similarities between the nth query and all of the keys.
The softmax function means that the key vectors “compete” with one another to contribute to the final result.
The queries and keys must have the same dimensions.
However, these can differ from the dimension of the values, which is usually the same size as the input, so the representation doesn’t change size.

Computing attention weights. a) Query vectors qn = βq + Ωqxn and key vectors kn = βk + Ωkxn are computed for each input xn. b) The dot products between each query and the three keys are passed through a softmax function to form non-negative attentions that sum to one. c) These route the value vectors (figure 12.1) via the sparse matrix from figure 12.2c.


Why separate query and key vectors?
The separation of query and key vectors allows the model to learn different representations for the purpose of matching queries to keys.
If the same vector were used for both queries and keys, the model would be limited to computing similarities based on a single representation.
By having separate projections, the model can learn to emphasize different aspects of the input when computing attention scores, leading to more flexible and expressive attention mechanisms.
Following examples illustrate how separate query and key vectors enable more flexible attention patterns.

Alice told Bob that he should leave because he was tired.
Focus on the first he.


Query: What does it seek? The first he seeks information about which male person it refers to, potentially Bob.
Key: What does it offer? The first he can serve as a useful reference for the second he, which may refer to the same person.


The cat with the white paws is sleeping.
Focus on cat.


Query: The noun cat may attend to white, paws, and the surrounding phrase to develop a richer representation of which cat is being discussed.
Key: The noun cat offers grammatical information to is, including that the subject is singular. Similarly, cat imposes constraints on what can show up later in the sentence. For example, it rules out wings as a possible continuation, since cats do not have wings.


The chef carefully prepared the meal.
Focus on prepared.


Query: The verb may seek its subject (chef) to determine who performed the action.
Key: The verb can offer information to meal, identifying the action performed on it.



Non-linearity in self-attention
Self-attention does not require an explicit activation function such as ReLU to introduce non-linearity. Although the queries, keys, and values are computed using linear transformations, the attention weights depend nonlinearly on the inputs.
Non-linearity enters in two places:

Dot-product scores. Each score combines a query and a key, both of which depend on \(\mathbf{X}\). Consequently, \(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\mathsf T}\) is quadratic in the input, rather than linear.
Softmax weights. Softmax exponentiates the scores and normalizes them so that the weights in each row sum to one. This is a nonlinear transformation of the scores.

Each output is a weighted sum of value vectors:
\[
\mathbf{y}_i=\sum_j \alpha_{ij}(\mathbf{X})\,\mathbf{v}_j.
\]
For fixed weights \(\alpha_{ij}\), this sum would be linear in the values. In self-attention, however, the weights themselves change with the input. Changing a word can therefore change both its value vector and how information is combined across the sequence. This dependence makes the overall mapping nonlinear.


Matrix form
The above computation can be written in a compact form if the N inputs \(\mathbf{x}_n\) form the columns of the D×N matrix \(\mathbf{X}\). The values, queries, and keys can be computed as:
\[\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbf{V}[\mathbf{X}] &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{v}\mathbf{1}^{T}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{\textit{v}}\mathbf{X}\nonumber \\
\mathbf{Q}[\mathbf{X}] &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{q}\mathbf{1}^{T}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{\textit{q}}\mathbf{X}\nonumber \\
\mathbf{K}[\mathbf{X}] &=& \boldsymbol\beta_{k}\mathbf{1}^{T}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{\textit{k}}\mathbf{X},
\end{eqnarray}\]
where \(\mathbf{1}\) is an N ×1 vector containing ones. The self-attention computation is then:
\[\begin{eqnarray}
  \mbox{{\bf Sa}}[\mathbf{X}] =\mathbf{V}[\mathbf{X}]\cdot\mbox{\bf Softmax}\Bigl[\mathbf{K}[\mathbf{X}]^{T}\mathbf{Q}[\mathbf{X}]\Bigr],
\end{eqnarray}\]
where the function \(\mbox{\bf Softmax}[•]\) takes a matrix and performs the softmax operation independently on each of its columns (figure 12.4). In this formulation, we have explicitly included the dependence of the values, queries, and keys on the input X to emphasize that self-attention computes a kind of triple product based on the inputs. However, from now on, we will drop this dependence and just write:
\[\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq:transformer_sa_matrix}
  \mbox{{\bf Sa}}[\mathbf{X}] =\mathbf{V}\cdot\mbox{\bf Softmax}\Bigl[\mathbf{K}^{T}\mathbf{Q}\Bigr].
\end{eqnarray}\]

Self-attention in matrix form. Self-attention can be implemented efficiently if we store the N input vectors xn in the columns of the D×N matrix X. The input X is operated on separately by the query matrix Q, key matrix K, and value matrix V. The dot products are then computed using matrix multiplication, and a softmax operation is applied independently to each column of the resulting matrix to calculate the attentions. Finally, the values are post-multiplied by the attentions to create an output of the same size as the input.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

The self-attention mechanism maps \(N\) inputs $ ^D $and returns \(x^{\prime} \in \mathbb{R}^D\) outputs .

np.random.seed(3)
# Number of inputs
N = 3
# Number of dimensions of each input
D = 4

# Print out the list

np.random.seed(0)

# Choose random values for the parameters
omega_q = np.random.normal(size=(D,D))
omega_k = np.random.normal(size=(D,D))
omega_v = np.random.normal(size=(D,D))
beta_q  = np.random.normal(size=(D,1))

beta_v  = np.random.normal(size=(D,1))

Now let’s compute the queries, keys, and values for each input

# Make three lists to store queries, keys, and values
all_queries = []
all_keys    = []
all_values  = []
# For every input
for x in all_x:
  # Compute the keys, queries and values.
  query = (omega_q @ x) + beta_q
  key   = (omega_k @ x) + beta_k
  value = (omega_v @ x) + beta_v

  all_queries.append(query)
  all_keys.append(key)
  all_values.append(value)

We’ll need a softmax function (equation 12.5) – here, it will take a list of arbitrary numbers and return a list where the elements are non-negative and sum to one

def softmax(items_in):

  # Compute the elements of items_out
  items_out = np.exp(items_in - np.max(items_in))
  items_out /= np.sum(items_out)

  return items_out ;

Now compute the self attention values:

all_x_prime = []

for n in range(N):
  # Create list for dot products of query N with all keys
  all_km_qn = []
  # Compute the dot products
  for key in all_keys:
    # Compute the appropriate dot product
    dot_product = all_queries[n].T @ key

    # Store dot product

  print(attention)

  for m in range(N):
    x_prime += attention[m] * all_values[m]

  all_x_prime.append(x_prime)

Now let’s compute the same thing, but using matrix calculations. We’ll store the inputs in the columns of a matrix, using equations 12.6 and 12.7/8.
Note: The book uses column vectors (for compatibility with the rest of the text), but in the wider literature it is more normal to store the inputs in the rows of a matrix; in this case, the computation is the same, but all the matrices are transposed and the operations proceed in the reverse order.

# Define softmax operation that works independently on each column
def softmax_cols(data_in):
  # Exponentiate all of the values
  exp_values = np.exp(data_in) ;
  # Sum over columns
  denom = np.sum(exp_values, axis = 0);
  # Replicate denominator to N rows
  denom = np.matmul(np.ones((data_in.shape[0],1)), denom[np.newaxis,:])
  # Compute softmax
  softmax = exp_values / denom
  # return the answer
  return softmax
     

 # Now let's compute self attention in matrix form
def self_attention(X,omega_v, omega_q, omega_k, beta_v, beta_q, beta_k):

  # 1. Compute queries, keys, and values
  # 2. Compute dot products
  # 3. Apply softmax to calculate attentions
  # 4. Weight values by attentions
  # Replace this line
  all_queries = (omega_q @ X) + beta_q
  all_keys    = (omega_k @ X) + beta_k
  all_values  = (omega_v @ X) + beta_v
  # X_prime = all_values @ softmax_cols(all_keys.T @ all_queries)
  X_prime = all_values @ softmax_cols(all_keys.T @ all_queries / np.sqrt(all_keys.shape[0]))


  return X_prime
     

# Copy data into matrix
X = np.zeros((D, N))
X[:,0] = np.squeeze(all_x[0])
X[:,1] = np.squeeze(all_x[1])
X[:,2] = np.squeeze(all_x[2])

# Run the self attention mechanism
X_prime = self_attention(X,omega_v, omega_q, omega_k, beta_v, beta_q, beta_k)

# Print out the results
print(X_prime)

# Now let's compute self attention in matrix form
def scaled_dot_product_self_attention(X,omega_v, omega_q, omega_k, beta_v, beta_q, beta_k):

  # 1. Compute queries, keys, and values
  # 2. Compute dot products
  # 3. Scale the dot products as in equation 12.9
  # 4. Apply softmax to calculate attentions
  # 5. Weight values by attentions
  # Replace this line
  all_queries = (omega_q @ X) + beta_q
  all_keys    = (omega_k @ X) + beta_k
  all_values  = (omega_v @ X) + beta_v

  X_prime = np.zeros_like(X)

  # Compute the dot products
  dot_products = all_queries.T @ all_keys
  # Scale the dot products
  scale_factor = np.sqrt(all_keys.shape[0])
  scaled_dot_products = dot_products / scale_factor
  # Apply softmax to calculate attentions
  attentions = softmax_cols(scaled_dot_products)
  # Weight values by attentions
  X_prime = (attentions @ all_values.T).T

  return X_prime
     

# Run the self attention mechanism
X_prime = scaled_dot_product_self_attention(X,omega_v, omega_q, omega_k, beta_v, beta_q, beta_k)

# Print out the results

title: Self-Attention
text:
Scaled dot-product self-attention

The passage compresses three ideas: why the dot products get large, why large inputs make softmax “saturate,” and why saturation kills gradients. Taking them in order:
1. Dot products grow with dimension
Suppose each component of a query \(\mathbf{q}\) and a key \(\mathbf{k}\) is roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1. That’s approximately true at initialization with standard weight init and normalized inputs. Their dot product is
\[\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k} = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i\]
Each term \(q_i k_i\) has mean 0 and variance 1, and you’re summing \(d_k\) of them. So the dot product has variance \(d_k\), or standard deviation \(\sqrt{d_k}\).
With \(d_k = 64\), typical attention logits are around ±8. With \(d_k = 512\), they’re around ±23. Nothing has been learned yet; the size comes purely from the dimension.
2. Large logits make softmax nearly one-hot
Softmax depends on the differences between its inputs, and it’s exponential in them. Compare one query’s logits against three keys:



logits
softmax output




[8, 0, −8] (unscaled, \(d_k=64\))
[0.9997, 0.0003, 0.0000001]


[1, 0, −1] (divided by \(\sqrt{64}=8\))
[0.665, 0.245, 0.090]



In the unscaled case, the query attends to one key and ignores everything else. The model never made that decision; it’s an artifact of the logit scale.
3. A one-hot softmax has near-zero gradients
This is the key step. Training works by asking: if I nudge this input a little, how much does the output change? That sensitivity is the gradient. If the answer is “barely at all,” the model gets almost no signal about which direction to adjust.
A nudge experiment. Take the logits from the example above and increase the second one by 1:










before nudge
after nudge
change in 2nd weight




Unscaled
[8, 0, −8] → weights [0.9997, 0.0003, 0.0000]
[8, 1, −8] → weights [0.9991, 0.0009, 0.0000]
+0.0006


Scaled
[1, 0, −1] → weights [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]
[1, 1, −1] → weights [0.468, 0.468, 0.063]
+0.22



The same nudge moves the scaled attention weight about 370 times more. When one logit dominates, softmax is “stuck”: the winner already has nearly all the weight and the others have nearly none, so small changes in either direction hardly register.
4. Why \(\sqrt{d_k}\) specifically
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) divides by the standard deviation of the dot product, which brings the variance back to 1 regardless of dimension:
\[\text{Var}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \frac{d_k}{d_k} = 1\]
Dividing by \(d_k\) would overshoot: the variance becomes \(1/d_k\), the logits all sit near zero, and attention becomes nearly uniform. Not scaling at all leaves softmax saturated. The \(\sqrt{d_k}\) factor is exactly what keeps logits in the range where softmax is sensitive.

section: Q0. Load and tokenize Tiny Stories
text:
Q0. Load and tokenize Tiny Stories
The following code prepares a text dataset for training a Masked Language Model (MLM) using a transformer encoder. It downloads a collection of short stories, tokenizes them using GPT-2’s tokenizer, and constructs a smaller vocabulary to make training more computationally efficient.
The code performs five main steps:


Load the TinyStories dataset
We use the TinyStories dataset, which contains short, relatively simple stories suitable for training small language models.
Rather than using the entire dataset, we select 50,000 stories for training and 5,000 for validation. The validation set will allow us to evaluate how well the model performs on stories it has not seen during training.
An end-of-text token is appended after each story to indicate where one story ends and another begins. This allows us to preserve story boundaries even though the stories are concatenated into a single token sequence.



Tokenize the stories
Neural networks operate on numbers rather than raw text. We therefore use GPT-2’s tokenizer, which employs byte-pair encoding (BPE), to convert text into sequences of integer token IDs.
The tokenize_stories function processes every story and concatenates its token IDs into one long sequence.



Construct a smaller vocabulary
GPT-2’s tokenizer has a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens. However, many of these tokens may occur very rarely in our relatively small training dataset.
We count how frequently each token appears in the training data and retain only tokens that occur at least five times.
This reduces the number of tokens the model needs to recognize and predict, which in turn reduces the number of parameters in the embedding and output layers.
We also reserve three special token IDs:








Token
ID
Purpose




[UNK]
0
Represents tokens excluded from the smaller vocabulary


[MASK]
1
Replaces selected tokens during masked language model training


[PAD]
2
Can be used to pad sequences to a common length



The retained GPT-2 tokens receive new IDs starting at 3.



Map between GPT-2 and local token IDs
We construct two dictionaries: gpt2_to_local and local_to_gpt2
The first converts original GPT-2 token IDs into IDs in our smaller vocabulary. The second performs the reverse mapping.
The encode function tokenizes new text and maps the resulting tokens into our vocabulary
Any token not included in our vocabulary is replaced by [UNK].
The decode function converts retained local token IDs back into readable text. Special tokens and unknown tokens are omitted because they have no corresponding entry in local_to_gpt2.
The encode function tokenizes new text and maps the resulting tokens into our vocabulary.

Prepare training and validation sequences
Finally, we convert the tokenized training and validation datasets into the smaller vocabulary:
We then report the number of tokens, the vocabulary size, and the proportion of validation tokens that became [UNK].
The validation UNK rate is particularly useful because it measures how often the model encounters tokens outside its vocabulary when processing unseen text.


import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import tiktoken

from collections import Counter
from datasets import load_dataset
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

tokenizer = tiktoken.get_encoding("gpt2")

SEQ_LEN = 128
BATCH_SIZE = 32

# A slice of TinyStories is plenty for a small model
train_ds = load_dataset("roneneldan/TinyStories", split="train[:50000]")
valid_ds = load_dataset("roneneldan/TinyStories", split="validation[:5000]")

def tokenize_stories(ds):
    ids = []
    for story in ds["text"]:
        ids.extend(tokenizer.encode_ordinary(story.strip()))
        ids.append(tokenizer.eot_token)   # marks the boundary between stories
    return ids

train_gpt2 = tokenize_stories(train_ds)
valid_gpt2 = tokenize_stories(valid_ds)

# Build a compact vocabulary from GPT-2 tokens that appear at least 5 times.
# Special tokens take the first IDs; PAD never appears in the data.
UNK_ID, MASK_ID, PAD_ID = 0, 1, 2
NUM_SPECIAL = 3

counts = Counter(train_gpt2)
kept = sorted(t for t, c in counts.items() if c >= 5)

gpt2_to_local = {t: i + NUM_SPECIAL for i, t in enumerate(kept)}
local_to_gpt2 = {i: t for t, i in gpt2_to_local.items()}
VOCAB_SIZE = len(kept) + NUM_SPECIAL

def encode(text):
    return [gpt2_to_local.get(t, UNK_ID) for t in tokenizer.encode_ordinary(text)]

def decode(ids):
    return tokenizer.decode([local_to_gpt2[i] for i in ids if i in local_to_gpt2])

train_tokens = [gpt2_to_local.get(t, UNK_ID) for t in train_gpt2]
valid_tokens = [gpt2_to_local.get(t, UNK_ID) for t in valid_gpt2]

print("Training tokens:  ", len(train_tokens))
print("Validation tokens:", len(valid_tokens))
